Scholars there are credited with calculating the Earth's circumference within a few percent, cataloguing star positions, and producing the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible called the Septuagint. About how many scrolls did it hold at its peak?
context: Eratosthenes was head librarian; he measured Earth's circumference from shadow differences between Alexandria and Aswan. The library declined gradually over centuries — Caesar's accidental harbour fire (48 BC), Aurelian's raid (273 AD), and Christian and Arab religious purges all played roles.

question: In the centre of the Moroccan city of Marrakech lies an old walled district whose markets have hummed since the 11th century. Pink-clay walls enclose alley networks of dyers, leather workers, slipper makers, and herbalists; at the heart sits a wide square that fills each evening with snake-charmers, storytellers, and food vendors. What is this central square called?
context: Marrakech was founded around 1070 by the Almoravid Berber empire. UNESCO recognises the square's oral storytelling tradition (halqa) as intangible heritage. The square's name means 'assembly of the dead' or 'end of the world' — etymology debated.

question: In the New City of Marrakech, behind cobalt-blue walls, lies a garden of cactuses, bamboo, and palms designed by French artist Jacques Majorelle between 1923 and 1947. The walls and pots are painted a vivid ultramarine the artist had trademarked. Saved from demolition in the 1980s by which fashion designer?
context: Saint Laurent bought the garden in 1980 with his partner Pierre Berge; he is buried in the rose garden there. His Berber Museum sits within the garden. The blue is now sold commercially as 'Majorelle Blue'.

question: In the medieval medina of Fes, Morocco, a mosque and madrasa founded by a wealthy young woman named Fatima al-Fihri in 859 AD became a centre of learning for medicine, astronomy, theology, and law. UNESCO and Guinness recognise it as the world's oldest continuously operating university. What is its name?
context: Fatima al-Fihri came from a wealthy merchant family that fled from Kairouan (Tunisia). She used her inheritance to build the mosque, then expanded it into a school. The Qarawiyyin library still holds a 9th-century Quran on gazelle parchment.

question: Founded in 670 AD by the Arab general Uqba ibn Nafi, this Tunisian inland city became the first major Islamic city in North Africa. Its Great Mosque, rebuilt over centuries on the original 7th-century foundations, has been called the model for almost every later mosque in the Maghreb. What is this city called?
context: Kairouan is considered Sunni Islam's fourth-holiest city after Mecca, Medina, and Jerusalem. Seven pilgrimages there were once said to equal one to Mecca. The mosque's prayer hall ceiling has 414 wooden support beams, one for each row of worshippers.

question: On the southern edge of the Sahara, where the Niger River meets the desert in modern Mali, a city flourished in the 13th-16th centuries as a meeting point of caravans, scholars, and salt-traders. It held three universities and as many as 700,000 manuscripts in private libraries — Arabic and Songhay texts on mathematics, astronomy, jurisprudence, and medicine. What is this city called?
context: When jihadist militants captured Timbuktu in 2012, librarians smuggled tens of thousands of manuscripts out to Bamako in oil drums, fertiliser sacks, and goat-hide bags. The manuscripts are now being digitised and slowly returned.

question: In the Ethiopian highlands, an early-medieval king ordered eleven monolithic churches carved directly down into the bedrock — entire buildings cut from a single block of rock, surrounded by trenches and connected by tunnels. The largest, Bete Medhane Alem, is the largest rock-hewn church in the world. After whom is this place named?
context: Bete Giyorgis (Church of Saint George), cut in the shape of a Greek cross from below, is the most photographed. Legend says angels worked alongside the masons at night. Local Orthodox Christians still worship in all eleven churches.

question: In northern Ethiopia, the ancient city of Aksum was the capital of a 1st-millennium AD kingdom whose ships sailed the Red Sea and whose rulers converted to Christianity around 330 AD. Carved single-stone granite stelae — some with false windows and doors representing multi-storey buildings — marked royal graves. How tall was the tallest?
context: Aksum stele number 1 fell during erection and lies in three pieces; it would have been the tallest single-piece stone monument ever raised. Mussolini took one stele to Rome in 1937; Italy returned it in 2005 after long pressure.

question: On the Barada river in Syria sits one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities on earth, mentioned in Egyptian texts before 1500 BC. Its Umayyad Mosque, built 706-715 AD, was the first monumental architectural achievement of Islam and stands over an older Roman temple of Jupiter and an older still Christian church. What is the city called?
context: The Umayyad Mosque preserves what tradition holds is the head of John the Baptist in a shrine inside the prayer hall — venerated by both Muslims and Christians. The Old City walls are mostly Roman foundations with medieval rebuilds.

question: In the central Syrian desert, halfway between Damascus and the Euphrates, an oasis city flourished as a caravan stop between the Roman Empire and Persia. In the 3rd century AD a warrior queen briefly rebelled against Rome, captured Egypt and most of Anatolia, then was defeated and brought to Rome in golden chains. Who was she?
context: Zenobia ruled Palmyra (Tadmor in Arabic) from about 267-272 AD. After her capture by the emperor Aurelian, she reportedly lived as a Roman noblewoman in Tivoli. ISIS destroyed major Palmyran monuments in 2015; restoration is partial.

question: Within Jerusalem's 16th-century Ottoman walls lies a square kilometre containing some of the most fought-over real estate on Earth: the Temple Mount, the Western Wall, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, and the Al-Aqsa Mosque, divided informally into four traditional quarters. What are the four quarters?
context: The Armenian Quarter is the smallest — a few thousand residents around the Cathedral of St James, established here since the 4th century. The Status Quo of 1852 freezes Christian denominational rights inside the Holy Sepulchre, governed by competing Greek Orthodox, Catholic, Armenian, Ethiopian, Coptic, and Syriac priests.

question: On the Temple Mount in Jerusalem stands an octagonal Islamic shrine completed in 691 AD, its golden dome visible across the Old City. Inside, a bedrock outcrop is venerated as the place where Abraham nearly sacrificed Isaac, and where Muhammad began his night journey. Who built it?
context: Abd al-Malik wanted a monumental statement of Islam in the heart of Jerusalem. The dome's exterior was originally lead-covered; the gold leaf today is from a Jordanian restoration in 1993-94. The interior mosaic inscriptions are among the oldest surviving Quranic texts.

question: Below the Temple Mount in Jerusalem stretches a 488-metre retaining wall, of which a 60-metre section is the holiest accessible site of modern Judaism — the only surviving piece of the platform that supported the Second Temple, destroyed by the Romans in 70 AD. Worshippers tuck folded paper prayers into the cracks between stones. What is this wall called in Hebrew?
context: The largest stone in the wall — the 'Western Stone' — weighs an estimated 570 tons. King Herod the Great's engineers placed it around 19 BC; how they moved it is still debated. Twice a year, paper prayers from the cracks are gathered and buried on the Mount of Olives.

question: In 8th-century Baghdad, the Abbasid caliphs founded a great translation and research institute that brought together Christian, Jewish, and Muslim scholars to translate Greek, Persian, and Indian texts into Arabic. Al-Khwarizmi (whose name gives us 'algorithm') and the Banu Musa brothers worked there. What was this institute called?
context: The House of Wisdom preserved the works of Aristotle, Galen, Ptolemy, Euclid, and Indian mathematicians during European Europe's early medieval period; many came back to Europe via Spanish translations of the Arabic. The Mongol sack of Baghdad in 1258 reportedly stained the Tigris black with library ink.

question: In central Iran stands one of the largest city squares in the world — a 510-by-160-metre rectangle laid out around 1602 by the Safavid shah Abbas I. It is enclosed on all sides by an architectural ensemble: a turquoise-tiled royal mosque, a smaller turquoise women's mosque, a palace, and a covered bazaar. What is this square called?
context: Shah Abbas moved the Safavid capital from Qazvin to Isfahan and personally supervised the new urban plan. The Persian proverb 'Isfahan is half the world' refers to the city at its 17th-century peak. The bazaar at the north end of the square still operates.

question: On the southern side of Isfahan's great square stands the masterpiece of Safavid architecture, completed in 1629 — a vast mosque whose 27-metre dome and twin 42-metre minarets are entirely covered in seven colours of glazed tile in floral and arabesque patterns. The acoustics under the dome are famous; whispers travel. What is it called today?
context: The dome and minarets are angled to face Mecca, set 45 degrees off the rest of the building, which faces the square. The seven-colour tile (haft-rangi) was a Safavid innovation faster than the older mosaic tilework but still spectacularly intricate.

question: On the edge of the central Iranian desert sits an old caravan city whose adobe houses are crowned with tall hollow towers — vertical chimneys with vents that catch even slight breezes and funnel them down into the rooms below, often passing over a basement pool to cool the air evaporatively. This ancient air conditioning has worked for 1,400 years. What is the city, and what are the towers called?
context: Yazd is the oldest brick city in the world, almost entirely built of mud brick. Its Zoroastrian community — the largest in Iran — still maintains a sacred fire that has reportedly burned for over 1,500 years.

question: In the highland capital of Yemen stretches an ancient walled city whose mud-brick tower houses, six and seven storeys tall, rise like dense forests of stalagmites. White-gypsum geometric patterns and frieze designs decorate the upper floors; the city has been continuously inhabited for over 2,500 years. What is its name?
context: Sana'a's tradition claims founding by Noah's son Shem. The Great Mosque, possibly the oldest still in continuous use anywhere, was built around 627 AD on the orders of the Prophet Muhammad. The civil war beginning 2014 has damaged many buildings; UNESCO has placed Sana'a on its List in Danger.

question: On the Persian Gulf, a 21st-century city stretched a slender three-lobed concrete-and-steel spire 828 metres into the sky in 2010 — the tallest human-made structure ever built. The shape is patterned after the geometry of the Hymenocallis desert flower. What is this tower called?
context: The Burj Khalifa is so tall it has different sunsets at different floors — observers on the 124th floor can watch the sun set, take an elevator up, and watch it set again. Concrete pours could only happen at night during summer because daytime temperatures hardened mixes too fast.

question: On the edge of the Kyzylkum desert in western Uzbekistan stands a compact walled old town — about 650 by 400 metres — where many of the buildings inside are 18th-19th-century mosques, minarets, palaces, and madrasas in soft sand-colour and turquoise tile. Walking it feels like walking inside a time capsule. What is this town called?
context: Khiva was the capital of a vicious slave-trading khanate until the Russians captured it in 1873. The Kalta Minor, a fat unfinished blue-tiled minaret stump, was meant to be the world's tallest; the khan who began it was killed in battle and his successor abandoned the project.

question: In the old city of Lahore, Pakistan, the largest mosque of the Mughal Empire — completed in 1673 under emperor Aurangzeb — accommodates 100,000 worshippers in its courtyard. Its red sandstone walls and three white-marble bulbous domes echo a pattern seen at the much earlier Taj Mahal. What is this mosque called?
context: The Badshahi was the largest mosque in the world for 313 years. Lahore Fort, directly across from it, is connected by an alley that once channelled royal elephants between palace and prayer.

question: On the bank of the Yamuna river in Old Delhi stands a vast red sandstone palace-fort completed in 1648 by Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, who moved his capital here from Agra. The marble pavilions inside were once inlaid with gemstones — most prized away by later invaders. What is this fort called?
context: Every Indian prime minister gives the Independence Day speech (15 August) from the Red Fort's ramparts. The Peacock Throne, encrusted with the Koh-i-Noor diamond, sat inside the Diwan-i-Khas until Persian invader Nadir Shah took it in 1739.

question: In a paradise-style charbagh garden in Delhi sits the tomb of the second Mughal emperor, completed in 1572 — a red sandstone domed building on a high terrace, with a Persian iwan entrance and white marble dome detailing. Its design is generally regarded as the prototype for a much more famous later monument. What was directly inspired by it?
choices: The Bibi Ka Maqbara in Aurangabad
context: Humayun's widow Bega Begum commissioned the tomb after his accidental death falling down library stairs in 1556. Persian architect Mirak Mirza Ghiyas designed it. Both Humayun's grandson Akbar and the dynasty's founder Babur came home to Delhi to rest here.

question: In central Jaipur stands an early-18th-century open-air observatory built by astronomer-king Sawai Jai Singh II — a complex of nineteen monumental masonry instruments, each designed to measure a specific aspect of the heavens with naked-eye precision. The largest, a 27-metre sundial, casts a shadow that moves 1 mm per second. What is this complex called?
context: 'Jantar Mantar' loosely means 'instruments and formulas'. Five such observatories were built by Jai Singh; the Jaipur one is the largest and best preserved. Their accuracy rivals contemporary European telescopic readings — but the king died before his work bore real astronomical fruit.

question: On the western bank of the Ganges, one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world descends in a series of stone-stepped landings to the river — eighty-eight of them, where pilgrims bathe at dawn, families cremate their dead at two of them, and the city has packed life and death into the same waterline for at least 3,000 years. What is this city called?
context: Hindus believe dying in Varanasi grants moksha — release from rebirth. The Manikarnika Ghat operates cremation fires that have reportedly burned continuously for at least 3,000 years. The city is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists (the Buddha gave his first sermon at nearby Sarnath), and Jains (one of the tirthankaras was born here).

question: In the heart of Kolkata, India, stands a white-marble domed building set in vast gardens — a 1921 imperial-British project intended as a memorial to Queen Victoria, but completed late enough that it served mostly as a museum from the start. The marble came from the same Rajasthan quarries as the Taj Mahal. What is it called?
context: Lord Curzon, viceroy of India, drove the project after Victoria's 1901 death. The dome is topped by a 5-metre bronze angel that pivots as a weather vane — the only one of its size in India. Kolkata was India's capital until 1911 when the British moved it to Delhi.

question: Mumbai's main railway station, completed in 1887 to mark Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee, is a flamboyant Victorian Gothic confection mixing Italian Gothic, Mughal motifs, and Indian sculpture — peacocks, monkeys, lions, and gargoyles in turreted red stone. Renamed in 1996, it now carries the name of which 17th-century Maratha king?
context: Frederick William Stevens designed it. The station — Mumbai's busiest, handling about three million commuters daily — has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2004. In November 2008 it was the scene of one of the Mumbai terror attacks.

question: Every weekday morning in Mumbai, roughly five thousand men in white caps collect about 200,000 home-cooked lunch boxes from suburban homes and deliver them — by cycle, train, and head-balanced carrying — to the right office desk in central Mumbai by noon, using a hand-painted alphanumeric code, with an estimated error rate of about one mistake per six million deliveries. What are these men called?
context: Established 1890 by Mahadeo Havaji Bachche. The system survives unchanged in Mumbai's vast public transport network. Six Sigma corporations study them; Prince Charles visited and was so impressed he invited them to his 2005 wedding.

question: In the central hill country of Sri Lanka sits a Buddhist temple complex that holds what tradition asserts is the Buddha's left upper canine tooth, brought from India in the 4th century AD. A daily ceremony of three drum-and-flute processions a day venerates the relic, which is locked in a series of nested gold caskets. What is this temple called?
context: Possession of the Tooth has historically conferred sovereignty over Sri Lanka. The relic was hidden underground when the Portuguese sacked Kandy in 1505; recovered, hidden again under the British, recovered again. The annual Esala Perahera procession draws a hundred elephants and tens of thousands of dancers.

question: Around the Kathmandu Valley in Nepal three former royal city-states each kept a 'durbar square' — a complex of palaces, courtyards, and pagoda temples in the layered tiered roof style developed in medieval Newari architecture. Carved wooden struts under the eaves depict gods, goddesses, and erotic scenes. The three cities are which?
context: All three durbar squares were damaged in the April 2015 earthquake; reconstruction continues. The carved wooden struts (tundal) of the Patan temples are among the finest medieval woodcarvings in Asia.

question: At the heart of Lhasa's old town sits the holiest temple in Tibetan Buddhism, founded in 642 AD to house a statue of the Buddha brought by the Chinese princess Wencheng on her marriage to Tibetan king Songtsen Gampo. Pilgrims walk a circumambulation route around the temple in three concentric rings called the Nangkhor, Barkhor, and Lingkhor. What is this temple called?
context: The statue inside — the Jowo Shakyamuni — is the most venerated image in Tibetan Buddhism. The Barkhor circuit around the temple is the most-walked pilgrimage path in Lhasa; pilgrims complete it daily, prostrating themselves full length on the stones.

question: In a vast underground complex near Xi'an, China, archaeologists in 1974 discovered some 8,000 life-size pottery soldiers — each face individually modelled — buried in formation to guard the tomb of the first emperor. Originally painted, the figures lost most of their colour to oxidation upon excavation. Whose tomb did they guard?
context: Local farmers digging a well found the first heads. The full tomb — a hill 76 metres high — has never been excavated; ancient texts describe an underground map of China with mercury rivers, and soil samples from the mound show mercury levels far above normal.

question: On the outskirts of Beijing lies a sprawling imperial pleasure garden — Longevity Hill rising over Kunming Lake, a 728-metre Long Corridor lined with 14,000 hand-painted scenes from Chinese legends, and a marble boat built by Empress Dowager Cixi from money allegedly diverted from the Chinese navy. What is this garden called?
context: Cixi's marble boat — pavilion-shaped, two-storeyed, never moves — became symbolic of late Qing decline. The Old Summer Palace nearby, looted and burned by British and French troops in 1860, was a different, even larger complex.

question: Inside Beijing's old city, threading between the larger boulevards, runs a network of narrow grey-brick alleys between courtyard houses called siheyuan — single-family compounds with rooms facing inward around an open central courtyard. The alleys have been there since the Yuan dynasty. What are these alleys called?
context: The word 'hutong' is a Mongolian loanword for 'water well' — the alleys were laid out around community wells when the Mongols founded Dadu (later Beijing) in the 13th century. Roughly two-thirds of Beijing's hutongs have been demolished since 1949 for high-rise development.

question: On the west bank of Shanghai's Huangpu river runs a kilometre of grand stone buildings built in the early 20th century, when European powers and the United States operated treaty-port concessions in the city. Banks, hotels, customs houses, and trading firms put up neoclassical, art deco, and Beaux-Arts piles. What is this riverfront called?
context: 'Bund' is an Anglo-Indian word for embankment, from Hindi bandh. Across the river in Pudong, a forest of supertall towers — Jin Mao, Shanghai World Financial Centre, Shanghai Tower — rose between 1999 and 2015 on what was farmland in 1990.

question: Above Hong Kong Island rises a 552-metre granite hill that has been the city's most expensive residential address since the 19th century — when the British colonial elite built mansions there to escape the tropical heat below. A funicular railway, opened in 1888, climbs through bamboo forest. What is this hill called?
context: The Peak Tram, the second funicular ever built in Asia, still uses original 19th-century gear in places. Pollution from Pearl River Delta industry frequently obscures Hong Kong's famous view today; the clearest days are after typhoons or in winter.

question: In Shanxi province in central China sits the best-preserved walled Ming-dynasty city anywhere — an intact 6-km city wall, 12 metres high and up to 5 metres thick, surrounding a grid of narrow streets and 17th-19th-century courtyard houses and merchant compounds. What is this city called?
context: Pingyao was the financial centre of Qing dynasty China — early modern banks (piaohao) that issued paper drafts were headquartered here, the Wall Street of Manchu-era China. The walls have 72 watchtowers and 3,000 crenellations representing Confucius's 72 disciples and 3,000 students.

question: In the foothills of the Himalayas in Yunnan, China, sits an old town of cobbled lanes, willow-shaded streams, and 13th-century waterways still running through the town centre. The indigenous Naxi people developed Dongba — the world's last surviving pictographic writing system actively used by religious specialists. What is this town called?
context: Lijiang sits at 2,400 metres in the shadow of Jade Dragon Snow Mountain. The Naxi people are matrilineal — until recently, women managed property and walking marriages. UNESCO listed the old town in 1997.

question: In central Tokyo, an intersection in front of a major railway station floods every two minutes with pedestrians crossing in all directions at once, including diagonally. Roughly 3,000 people may cross at the peak of a single light cycle. Around it, multi-storey video screens broadcast advertising at the crowd. What is this intersection called?
context: About 2,500 people cross per cycle off-peak; over 3,000 at peak — perhaps a quarter million per day. The statue of the loyal dog Hachiko, who waited for his dead owner at Shibuya station from 1925 to 1935, stands at the south exit.

question: At the centre of Tokyo, surrounded by moats and concentric stone walls, sits the home of the Japanese imperial family — a vast park where the city's largest contiguous green space is otherwise mostly off-limits to the public. The grounds were the site of the much older Edo Castle, the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns. What is the modern complex called?
context: During Japan's 1980s bubble, the land of the Imperial Palace was reportedly worth more than all the real estate in California combined. Only the East Gardens — the old fortress kernel — are normally open to the public.

question: Until 2018, the largest fish market in the world operated in central Tokyo, with a pre-dawn tuna auction where huge whole bluefin sold for tens of thousands of dollars each. The inner wholesale market then moved to Toyosu; the outer market, with its prepared-food shops, dried-fish stalls, and sushi counters, stayed. What was this market called?
context: Tsukiji at peak handled about 2,000 tons of seafood daily. A record bluefin sold in 2019 (at the new Toyosu site) went for ¥333 million — about $3 million for a single fish. The outer market at Tsukiji is still full of small specialty shops.

question: On the outskirts of Kyoto sits a Buddhist temple whose top two floors are covered in real gold leaf, reflecting in the still water of a carefully arranged pond garden. Originally built in 1397 as a retirement villa for the shogun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, it was burned to the ground by an unstable monk in 1950 and rebuilt to original specifications. What is it called?
context: Novelist Yukio Mishima's 1956 novel The Temple of the Golden Pavilion fictionalised the arsonist's motive. The reconstructed pavilion has thicker gold-leaf than the original — five times as thick, applied in 1987. The phoenix on the roof is the original 1397 piece.

question: In southern Kyoto, a long path winds up Mount Inari through a forest of bright vermillion-orange torii gates — about 10,000 of them — donated over centuries by Japanese individuals and companies, each inscribed with the donor's name and date. The path is sacred to the Shinto god of rice and merchants. What is this shrine called?
context: The earliest gates date from 711 AD. White stone foxes — kitsune, the messengers of Inari — flank gates and altars along the path. The full climb takes about two hours; pilgrims have been making it for over a thousand years.

question: On Kyoto's western outskirts lies a riverside district famous for a path through a dense grove of moso bamboo, the stems 20-30 metres tall, the canopy filtering sound into a particular quiet rustle the Japanese government has officially named one of the 100 Soundscapes of Japan. What is this district called?
context: Moso bamboo (Phyllostachys edulis) is a single species; the grove is one rhizome system 'planted' from a few rhizomes centuries ago. The Togetsukyo Bridge ('Moon-Crossing Bridge') at the foot of Arashiyama Mountain has been replaced many times since the 9th century.

question: In the Gion district of Kyoto, around the willow-shaded Shirakawa stream, women trained from teenage years in classical dance, shamisen, tea ceremony, and the art of conversation move discreetly between exclusive teahouses on wooden geta clogs. They are recognised by their formal kimonos and high-painted faces. What are they called in Kyoto?
context: In Kyoto, the formal terms are 'geiko' (senior) and 'maiko' (apprentice); 'geisha' is more Tokyo usage. There are perhaps 250 actively working geiko/maiko today; in 1925 there were about 80,000 across Japan.

question: In the Kansai region city of Nara — Japan's capital from 710 to 794 — sits one of the largest bronze statues in the world: a 15-metre seated Buddha cast in 752 AD, housed in the wooden hall of Todai-ji, which was for centuries the largest wooden building on Earth. About how many tons of bronze went into the casting?
context: The casting nearly bankrupted the imperial state — about half the country's bronze of that decade went into it. The hall has been twice destroyed by fire and rebuilt smaller; the current building is from 1709 and is still the world's largest historical wooden building.

question: In Hiroshima's Peace Park stands the burnt-out skeleton of a domed reinforced-concrete building, almost directly under the hypocentre of the 6 August 1945 atomic bombing. The building's location 160 metres from ground zero meant the blast wave hit it almost vertically — it stood while almost everything around it was vaporised. What was the building called before the war?
context: Designed by Czech architect Jan Letzel in 1915. The decision to preserve the ruin — declared a Peace Memorial in 1966, World Heritage in 1996 — was contested; many survivors initially wanted it demolished as too painful a reminder.

question: In the wooded mountains north of Tokyo, an elaborately carved and gilded shrine honours the deified founder of the Tokugawa shogunate. The complex includes a five-storey pagoda, hundreds of stone and bronze lanterns, and a richly painted gate considered the masterpiece of late Edo decorative carving. Who is the shrine dedicated to?
context: Nikko Toshogu was begun by Tokugawa Hidetada in 1617 and lavishly expanded by Ieyasu's grandson Iemitsu. The 'See no, hear no, speak no evil' three-monkey panel is a small section of the shrine's stables. Japanese folklore says 'never say splendid before seeing Nikko'.

question: In central Taipei rises a white-marble octagonal mausoleum with a blue tile roof and a 25-metre-tall bronze seated figure inside. The forty-foot-high plaza in front of it is the largest such ceremonial space in Taiwan, used both for honour-guard ceremonies and protest movements. After whom is it named?
context: Completed 1980. The plaza's name was changed to 'Liberty Square' in 2007 under President Chen Shui-bian's administration. The hall is now also the site of the National Concert Hall and National Theatre, in a unified arts plaza.

question: Halfway between Hanoi and Saigon along Vietnam's coast sits the former imperial capital of the Nguyen dynasty (1802-1945). A 10-kilometre stone wall encloses the Imperial City, with a yellow-roofed Forbidden Purple City inside — modelled deliberately on Beijing's Forbidden City, but Vietnamised in scale and detail. What was this capital called?
context: Hue was devastated in the 1968 Tet Offensive; many buildings of the Forbidden Purple City inside were destroyed. UNESCO has listed the surviving complex; reconstruction continues. The Perfume River (Song Huong) runs through the city.

question: On a small section of Vietnam's central coast sits a 15th-19th-century trading port whose Japanese, Chinese, and Vietnamese merchants left a fusion of architectural styles in a tight low-rise old quarter. Every full-moon night, electric lights are switched off and the streets are lit only by colourful silk lanterns hung from every house. What is this town called?
context: The Japanese Covered Bridge (1593) survives; the Chinese assembly halls are still active. The Thu Bon river silted up in the late 19th century, ending Hoi An's role as a port — which is why it remained perfectly preserved when the trade moved to Da Nang.

question: The town of Siem Reap in northern Cambodia is the gateway to one of the largest religious monument complexes in the world — a sprawling temple plain that was the capital of the Khmer Empire from the 9th to the 15th century. The single most famous temple, originally a 12th-century Hindu temple to Vishnu, is what?
context: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument by area on Earth — about 162 hectares. Its outline appears on the Cambodian flag. The Khmer Empire at its peak (around 1200 AD) ruled most of mainland Southeast Asia and supported a metropolitan area of perhaps a million people.

question: In the former Burmese capital of Yangon rises a 99-metre gilded stupa atop Singuttara Hill, said by tradition to enshrine eight hairs of the Buddha given by the Buddha himself to two merchant brothers. Above the bell-shape rises a hti — an umbrella spire covered in gold, encrusted with thousands of diamonds, rubies, and sapphires. What is this stupa called?
context: Successive Burmese rulers have re-gilded the Shwedagon, adding their own weight in gold; the current covering is over 50 tons of gold leaf. The 76-carat Naung Yan diamond sits at the tip of the hti, where it catches the first and last sunlight.

question: On the south coast of Singapore Island, a 35-hectare district built entirely on reclaimed land hosts an architectural icon: three 55-storey hotel towers supporting a 343-metre cantilevered ship-shaped sky-park with an infinity pool that appears to flow off the building's edge. Completed in 2010 and designed by Moshe Safdie. What is this building called?
context: The infinity pool sits 191 metres up and uses computer-controlled level adjustment so guests can swim without strange sway. The whole development is built on land that did not exist in 1980 — Singapore has expanded its land area by about 25% since independence through reclamation.

question: Adjacent to Marina Bay Sands, a 101-hectare park hosts steel-framed 'supertree' structures up to 50 metres tall, covered in living plants and lit at night by computer-coordinated colour. Two glass biomes — the Cloud Forest and the Flower Dome — house the world's largest indoor waterfall and the largest column-free glasshouse. What is this park called?
context: The 18 Supertrees host vertical gardens of over 162,900 plants from 200 species. Cooling tubes run through the trunks; the biggest Supertrees gather solar energy and serve as exhaust vents for the climate-controlled biomes nearby.

question: In Indonesia's capital, a small district preserves the colonial-era buildings of the Dutch East India Company's Asian headquarters — Stadhuis (city hall, 1710), Cafe Batavia, the old port at Sunda Kelapa, and several Dutch-built canals. Most of the rest of Dutch Batavia was demolished by Sukarno's post-independence government. What is this district called?
context: The VOC (Dutch East India Company) chose the site in 1619, expelling the Sundanese kingdom that had ruled there. Sunda Kelapa harbour still functions as a working port for traditional Indonesian Bugis schooners (pinisi).

question: On the Indonesian island of Java, near Yogyakarta, sits a vast 9th-century Buddhist monument: 504 statues of the Buddha, nine stacked terraces ascending to a central stupa, the whole structure shaped like a three-dimensional Buddhist cosmological diagram. Pilgrims walk a clockwise spiral path around each level. What is this monument called?
context: Built around 825 AD under the Sailendra dynasty; buried under volcanic ash and jungle for centuries, rediscovered in 1814 by Sir Stamford Raffles. UNESCO-led international rescue (1975-82) dismantled and reassembled much of the lower galleries to fix groundwater damage.

question: About 17 km from Borobudur on Java, a 9th-century Hindu temple complex thrusts skyward in slender stone spires up to 47 metres tall — three central temples dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva, surrounded by hundreds of smaller temples, many earthquake-shattered and slowly being rebuilt. What is this complex called?
context: Prambanan and Borobudur were built within fifty years of each other by rival dynasties (Hindu Sanjaya and Buddhist Sailendra), now an UNESCO inscription pair. Java holds the densest concentration of monumental Hindu-Buddhist temple ruins outside South Asia.

question: On the southern tip of Bali, a cliffside Hindu temple has guarded the island spiritually since the 11th century, perched on a 70-metre sea-cliff watching over the Indian Ocean. Daily kecak dances of bare-chested chanting men — no instruments, only voice — perform the Ramayana at sunset on a stone stage facing the sea. What is this temple called?
context: Uluwatu is one of the six 'kahyangan' temples — directional sentinel temples guarding Bali from spiritual threat. The aggressive long-tailed macaques on the path are notorious for stealing visitors' sunglasses and trading them back for fruit.

question: Inside the modern megacity of Manila a 64-hectare walled district preserves what is left of the original Spanish colonial city, founded in 1571. Stone walls 6 metres thick once enclosed Spanish governmental buildings, friars' churches, and the city's only public spaces. Most of what is left dates from the 1945 Battle of Manila, which destroyed most of the area. What is this district called?
context: The Battle of Manila (February-March 1945) killed roughly 100,000 civilians and flattened Manila as completely as Warsaw. San Agustin Church inside Intramuros survived; it is the oldest stone church in the Philippines (1607).

question: On the cool central highlands of Ethiopia at 2,355 metres sits the diplomatic capital of the African continent — host city of the African Union headquarters (since 2002) and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. The name in Amharic means 'new flower'. Whose 1886 imperial decision established this city as the capital?
answer: Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu
choices: Emperor Menelik II and Empress Taytu
Emperor Haile Selassie and Empress Menen
context: Empress Taytu reportedly chose the site for its hot springs. Addis Ababa is one of the highest capitals in the world; its altitude gives it a permanent springlike climate despite sitting only 9 degrees from the equator.

question: In eastern Ethiopia, an old walled city is considered Islam's fourth holiest, said to contain 82 mosques (three from the 10th century) and 102 shrines within its 5-metre-thick walls. Hyenas have been hand-fed at the city gates each night for over a century — a custom protecting both the hyenas and the people. What is this city called?
context: Arthur Rimbaud lived in Harar from 1880 to 1891 as a coffee and weapons trader. The hyena feeding probably has its origin in a 19th-century famine when hyenas were attacking children; the night feedings keep them satiated outside the walls.

question: On the Bight of Benin in west Africa sprawls one of the world's fastest-growing megacities — over 20 million people, on a series of islands and lagoons. It is the financial and entertainment capital of Africa's most populous country and home to the third-largest film industry in the world. What is the city, and what is the film industry called?
context: Lagos lost its position as Nigeria's capital to Abuja in 1991 but remains the economic heart. Nollywood now produces roughly 2,500 films a year, mostly direct-to-video and streaming — second only to India's Bollywood by output.

question: Off the coast of Senegal, a small basalt island half a kilometre wide once held a House of Slaves built around 1776 — a pink-walled building with a 'Door of No Return' opening directly onto the Atlantic, through which captives were loaded onto ships bound for the Americas. Pope John Paul II and Barack Obama have both visited. What is this island called?
context: Goree Island is contested: historians debate how many enslaved people actually passed through this specific island compared to other West African ports. But the memorial role is now well-established — it became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.

question: In the capital of Ghana stands a 1957 commemorative arch and adjacent square marking the first sub-Saharan African colony to gain independence from European rule. The Black Star at the top of the arch became the symbol of Pan-African pride; the square hosts the country's independence-day parades. After whom is the arch named?
context: Ghana's Black Star also appears on its flag and gives the national football team its nickname. Nkrumah's Pan-African vision aimed to unite the continent — Black Star Square hosted leaders such as Lumumba, Mandela, Nyerere, and Nasser in the early 1960s.

question: In the central forest of Ghana sits the spiritual capital of the Ashanti, a kingdom that maintained independence from European powers longer than almost any other African state. Its rulers still preside over the Golden Stool — a sacred object believed to embody the soul of the Ashanti nation. What is this city called?
context: The British fought four wars against the Ashanti (1824-1900) before finally subduing them. Queen Mother Yaa Asantewaa led the last (1900) revolt, fighting for the Golden Stool — which had been demanded as a seat for the British governor.

question: On the Congo river — the world's deepest river — sprawls the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a sprawling metropolis of about 17 million people. Across the river, just three kilometres away, sits the capital of a different country. What unusual geographic distinction does this pair hold?
answer: Closest pair of national capitals on opposite banks of one river
choices: Closest pair of national capitals on opposite banks of one river
Only city pair connected by submarine tunnel under a river
Only city pair sharing one elected mayor across two states
Closest national capitals in the same continent on land
context: Kinshasa (DRC) and Brazzaville (Republic of the Congo) face each other across the Pool Malebo of the Congo river. Vatican City and Rome are technically closer, but Vatican is not a typical 'capital'.

question: South Africa's largest city was founded in 1886 — a year that the discovery of a particular metal triggered the largest mineral rush in African history. The gold-bearing reef stretches some 400 km underground in an arc; mines under the city descend to depths over 4 kilometres. What is this gold-bearing reef called?
context: About 40% of all the gold ever mined in human history came from the Witwatersrand. Johannesburg sits on the Highveld plateau at 1,750 metres; the climate is mild despite being on the African continent, thanks to elevation.

question: On South Africa's east coast sits a port city with the largest population of South Asian descent outside Asia itself. Indentured Indian labourers were brought to work the colony's sugar plantations beginning in 1860; Mahatma Gandhi practised law there for twenty-one years. What is this city called?
context: Gandhi's brutal experience being thrown off a train in nearby Pietermaritzburg (1893) for sitting in first class radicalised him. The Bunny Chow — a hollowed-out loaf filled with curry — was invented in Durban as a takeaway lunch for Indian sugar-cane workers.

question: The capital of Madagascar sits at 1,275 metres on a central plateau, its skyline dominated by the brick-and-stone Royal Palace (Rova) on the highest hill. Below, terraced rice paddies climb the surrounding slopes — irrigated farming brought from Southeast Asia about 1,500 years ago when the island was settled. What is the city called?
context: 'Antananarivo' means 'city of the thousand' in Malagasy. The Royal Palace burned down in 1995 (likely arson); restoration is ongoing. Malagasy is a language of the Austronesian family — closer to Indonesian than to any African language.

question: Above the Mother City of South Africa rises a flat-topped sandstone massif 1,086 metres high, often covered by a 'tablecloth' of orographic cloud spilling over its edge. Six hundred million years old (so older than nearly all other mountains on Earth), it holds more plant species than the entire United Kingdom. What is this mountain called?
context: Table Mountain's fynbos vegetation forms part of the Cape Floral Kingdom — the smallest of the world's six floral kingdoms, but among the most species-rich. A cableway has run up the mountain since 1929.

question: On the West African coast, the capital of Togo sits beside what is sometimes called the world's largest fetish market — herbs, animal parts, sculpted figurines, and ritual objects used in the traditional religion of southern Togo, Benin, and southwestern Nigeria. What religion is this?
context: Vodun originated among the Fon and Ewe peoples of Benin and Togo. The Atlantic slave trade carried it to Haiti (as Vodou), Cuba (as Santeria), and Brazil (as Candomble). About 40% of Togolese still practise some form of Vodun today.

question: On Lake Nokoue near Benin's economic capital sits the largest lake village in Africa — about 30,000 people living in stilt houses, with everything (markets, schools, churches, mosques, even cemeteries) on raised platforms. Founded in the 17th century by the Tofinu people fleeing slave raids from the Fon kingdom. What is this village called?
context: Fon religious belief reportedly prevented warriors from attacking people on water; the Tofinu exploited this protection. Today Ganvie's economy is part fishing, part tourism. Children paddle pirogues to school on the lake.

question: The capital of Tunisia preserves one of the largest and oldest medieval Islamic city centres in North Africa, founded in 698 AD. Inside its 4-kilometre-long Hafsid-era walls lie 700 monuments — including the Zaytuna Mosque, university, and one of the most extensive souks in the Arab world. What is the medina of Tunis called?
context: The Zaytuna Mosque (founded 698) is one of the oldest universities in the world. The medina is UNESCO-listed since 1979. Just outside the walls sits the ruined site of ancient Carthage — the Phoenician city Rome destroyed in 146 BC.

question: In Manhattan, an 843-acre rectangle of designed wilderness was carved out in 1858, when the city was still mostly south of 42nd Street, by clearing a working-class neighbourhood called Seneca Village. The two designers chose meandering paths, lakes, and rolling lawns rather than a formal European parterre. Who were they?
answer: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux
choices: Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux
Frederick Law Olmsted and Daniel Burnham
context: Olmsted is considered the founder of American landscape architecture. Central Park's land was acquired by the city via eminent domain; Seneca Village had been New York City's largest community of free Black property owners.

question: In midtown Manhattan, a Beaux-Arts railway terminal completed in 1913 has a famous painted ceiling depicting the constellations of the Mediterranean sky as seen in a medieval manuscript — painted backwards. The terminal has 67 tracks on two levels and is the largest railway station in the world by platform count. What is it called?
context: The reversed constellations are explained variously as a copy from a medieval source that showed the sky as God would see it, or simply a mistake. Either way, the ceiling was lovingly restored in 1998 after tobacco smoke had blackened it; a small dirty patch was left visible.

question: Inside a red-brick Georgian building on the second floor of which Independence Hall served as the Pennsylvania State House, the Continental Congress voted on 4 July 1776 to adopt the Declaration of Independence. The same room hosted the 1787 Constitutional Convention. In which city does this building stand?
context: The Liberty Bell — cracked across one side — was originally cast in 1752 to hang in the Pennsylvania State House steeple. It got its 'Liberty' name from 1830s abolitionists; the bell now sits in a glass pavilion across the street from Independence Hall.

question: The American federal capital was laid out in 1791 on a square of land carved from Maryland and Virginia, with radial avenues named for the states crossing a Cartesian grid. The principal designer — born in France, a major in the Continental Army — was fired by President Washington for refusing to compromise his plan. Who was he?
context: L'Enfant's plan was largely ignored after his dismissal but rediscovered and substantially restored in the 1901 McMillan Plan. The Black mathematician Benjamin Banneker helped Ellicott complete the original survey from memory after L'Enfant left with the plans.

question: The American National Mall is a 3-km grassy axis from the United States Capitol building in the east to the Lincoln Memorial in the west. Roughly halfway along stands a 169-metre obelisk in three differently coloured bands of marble — a darker stripe marks where construction stopped during the Civil War. What is the obelisk called?
context: Construction began in 1848 and resumed in 1879; the second batch of marble came from a different quarry and weathered to a different colour. The obelisk was the tallest building in the world from 1884 to 1889 (when the Eiffel Tower opened).

question: Around 1900, the city of Chicago undertook one of the largest civil engineering projects of the 19th century: it reversed the flow of the Chicago River, away from Lake Michigan (the city's drinking-water source) and into the Mississippi watershed (via the Sanitary and Ship Canal). Why was this done?
answer: Sewage was polluting Chicago's drinking water from Lake Michigan
choices: Sewage was polluting Chicago's drinking water from Lake Michigan
Lake Michigan was rising and threatening downtown flooding
The river was too shallow for navigation to nearby Wisconsin
The city needed lower-cost shipping access to the Atlantic
context: Chicago's untreated sewage flushing into Lake Michigan caused massive cholera and typhoid outbreaks. The reversal sent it downstream — to the protest of St Louis, which sued and lost. The project required deepening of the Chicago Sanitary and Ship Canal.

question: Around 1900, in a particular New Orleans neighbourhood centred on Storyville (the city's official red-light district) and Congo Square (where African slaves had been allowed to drum on Sundays), African, Creole, and European musical traditions fused into a syncopated improvisational style. Cornetist Buddy Bolden was reportedly the first to lead a band in the new sound. What is the genre called?
context: Congo Square is the only place in the antebellum American South where enslaved people were legally permitted to drum — a legacy of Louisiana's French Catholic Code Noir, less restrictive than Anglo-Protestant slave codes elsewhere. The drumming preserved West African polyrhythms central to jazz.

question: The oldest district of New Orleans was laid out in 1718 by French colonists; most of its current buildings date from after the 1788 and 1794 fires, which were rebuilt in Spanish Colonial style (lacy iron balconies, interior courtyards). The neighbourhood sits about three feet above sea level — and survived Katrina better than newer districts. What is its French and English name?
context: Vieux Carre means 'Old Square'. Most of its land is just above the Mississippi River's natural levee, so it sits relatively high and dry. Most of New Orleans is below sea level, and was built on drained swamp.

question: On a 9-hectare island in San Francisco Bay, surrounded by strong cold currents, sat a federal prison from 1934 to 1963 holding America's most dangerous convicts — Al Capone, Machine Gun Kelly, Robert 'Birdman' Stroud. Only one set of escapees may have made it across to the mainland (the case remains officially unsolved). What is the island called?
context: The name comes from Spanish 'alcatraces' (pelicans), the original Spanish name for the bird-covered rock. Three prisoners (Frank Morris and the Anglin brothers) escaped in 1962 using a raft of raincoats; their bodies were never found, and the FBI officially closed the case in 1979.

question: San Francisco is the only city in the world that still operates the cable-car system invented by Andrew Smith Hallidie in 1873 — wooden cars gripping onto a continuously moving steel cable buried just below the street, powered by a central winding house. Why was the system invented?
answer: Horses kept dying climbing the city's steep hills
choices: Horses kept dying climbing the city's steep hills
The streets were too narrow for trolley overhead wires
Electric streetcars failed in San Francisco's salt air
The city banned all combustion-engine vehicles
context: Hallidie had reportedly seen a horse slip and be dragged down a hill by a falling carriage. The cable car system once spread to Seattle, Chicago, and Sydney; only San Francisco's three lines survived to become a National Historic Landmark.

question: On a peninsula jutting north from downtown Vancouver lies an urban park larger than New York's Central Park — 405 hectares of mostly intact temperate rainforest, encircled by a 9-km seawall promenade. The park was dedicated in 1888 to a British Governor-General. Who?
context: Stanley also donated the Stanley Cup for ice hockey championship. The cedars in Stanley Park are second growth; the original forest was logged before the park designation, but some trees are over 800 years old. The seawall took 60 years to construct (1917-1980).

question: On the Lake Ontario waterfront rises a 553-metre concrete telecommunications tower completed in 1976 — the tallest free-standing structure in the world for 33 years until the Burj Khalifa surpassed it. Its observation deck includes a glass floor that lets visitors look straight down 342 metres. What is this tower called?
context: CN stands for Canadian National (the railway). The tower was built to broadcast over Toronto's growing forest of skyscrapers, which were causing reception problems. Each year about 2 million people visit; the EdgeWalk lets adventurous types walk hands-free around the outer edge of the main pod.

question: Mexico City is built on the rubble of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital that Cortes razed in 1521. The original city sat on an island in a vast saline lake — Lake Texcoco — connected to shore by raised causeways. The Spanish drained the lake; the modern city is still slowly sinking into the soft former lakebed. About how many people lived in Tenochtitlan at its peak?
context: Tenochtitlan was probably larger than any European city in 1500 — larger than London or Paris. The Spanish conquistadors compared it to Venice. Cortes had perhaps 800 men plus tens of thousands of indigenous allies; the city fell after a 93-day siege and smallpox outbreak.

question: Mexico City's central square is one of the largest public squares in the world — 240 by 240 metres of open paving, dominated by a Spanish cathedral, the presidential palace, and the supreme court, with the Aztec Templo Mayor ruins exposed in the corner. The square sits exactly atop the Aztec ceremonial centre. What is this square called?
context: The Zocalo was once the Mexican ceremonial centre where Tenochtitlan's twin pyramid temples stood. The cathedral was deliberately built atop the demolished Templo Mayor; foundations dug in 1978 hit the buried Aztec ruins, now exhumed and open to visitors.

question: On Colombia's Caribbean coast sits a walled colonial city founded by Spain in 1533 that became Spain's main treasure port for South American silver. Its 11 km of stone walls, completed in 1796, withstood multiple pirate sieges (including the 1741 attack by the Royal Navy under Edward Vernon, who brought 23,000 men and lost most of them to yellow fever). What is this city called?
context: The city's San Felipe de Barajas fortress is one of the largest Spanish fortifications in the Americas. The 1741 siege failure is sometimes credited with preserving Spanish South America from English domination. Gabriel Garcia Marquez set Love in the Time of Cholera (1985) here.

question: The capital of Ecuador sits at 2,850 metres on the slopes of an active volcano, just 25 km south of the equator. Its old town — UNESCO's first-ever World Heritage listing in 1978 — contains 130 monumental colonial-era buildings and 5,000 colonial houses in a remarkably intact 16th-18th-century urban fabric. What active volcano does Quito sit beside?
context: Pichincha last erupted in 1999 with an ash column but no lava reaching Quito. The volcano is technically active. Quito's altitude makes it one of the highest capitals in the world and gives it spring-like temperatures year-round despite its equatorial latitude.

question: In the Peruvian Andes at 3,400 metres sits the former capital of the Inca Empire, organised in the layout of a puma (its head being the Sacsayhuaman fortress). After Pizarro's conquest in 1533, Spanish baroque churches were built directly on the foundations of Inca temples; you can still see the perfectly fitted Inca stones below the colonial structures. What is the city's name?
context: The Coricancha (Golden Temple) of the Inca sun god was looted and overlaid with the Santo Domingo monastery; both layers are visible in the same building. Cusco was the political and ceremonial centre of an empire that ran from southern Colombia to central Chile.

question: Above Cusco on a hill sit the ruins of an Inca complex of three concentric zigzag walls of huge polygonal stones — some weighing over 100 tons — fitted together so precisely that a knife blade cannot pass between them, with no mortar. What is this site called?
context: Spaniards quarried Sacsayhuaman for centuries to build colonial Cusco below; only the largest stones — too big to move — survived. The walls form the head of the puma in the Inca city plan. Twenty thousand workers reportedly built it over decades in the 1400s.

question: On a saddle between two peaks high in the Andes at 2,430 metres sits an Inca royal estate built around 1450, abandoned about a century later, and never found by the Spanish. It was 'rediscovered' for the outside world in 1911 by Yale historian Hiram Bingham, who was actually looking for a different lost city. What was the site called?
context: Bingham was looking for Vilcabamba — the last Inca stronghold against the Spanish. Local farmers had already known about and partially cultivated Machu Picchu, but the site was unknown to historians. The royal estate was probably built by emperor Pachacuti.

question: On the dry coastal plain of southern Peru, a 450-square-kilometre stretch of red-brown desert is etched with hundreds of straight lines, geometric shapes, and recognisable animal figures (a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider, a whale) — best seen from the air. They were made by the Nazca culture between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD by clearing surface stones to reveal lighter soil. What is this complex called?
context: The largest figures span 200 metres or more. Scholarly theories about their purpose vary: ritual paths, astronomical alignments, water-source markers, and offerings to mountain gods are all proposed. The lines have survived because Nazca gets less than 4 mm of rain a year.

question: The capital of Peru — founded by Pizarro in 1535 — has, scattered across its modern districts, about 400 surviving pre-Inca adobe-brick pyramid mounds, some over 1,500 years old. They predate the Inca and represent the older Lima, Maranga, and Ychma cultures. What are these pyramid mounds locally called?
context: Huaca Pucllana, in the Miraflores district, is the most-visited example — a 25-metre stepped pyramid in the middle of an upscale neighborhood. Huaca means 'sacred place' or 'sacred thing' in Quechua, a broader category than just monuments.

question: Bolivia's seat of government sits in a canyon at altitudes ranging from 3,200 to 4,100 metres — the city flows up and down the canyon walls in stacks of red-brick houses. A modern aerial-cable-car network (the Mi Teleferico, 30+ km) functions as urban transit between the cliffside neighbourhoods. What is the city called?
context: La Paz is the highest de facto capital in the world. Sucre is technically Bolivia's constitutional capital, but the government has met in La Paz since 1898. The Mi Teleferico — built 2014-2019 — has been an instant transport success; rush-hour cars come every 12 seconds.

question: On the eastern coast of Brazil sits the original capital of colonial Brazil (1549-1763), whose old quarter is a 16th-18th-century kaleidoscope of pastel baroque mansions and Catholic churches gilded in extraordinary quantities of leaf — the result of a sugar economy worked by enslaved Africans. The quarter, named for an iconic post used for slave whippings, is now UNESCO-listed. What is the old quarter called?
context: Pelourinho preserves much of Brazil's African Bahian heritage — capoeira, the syncretic Candomble religion, and dishes like moqueca and acaraje. The Church of Sao Francisco contains about 800 kg of gold leaf — one of the most extravagantly gilded interiors in the world.

question: Each year before Lent, Rio de Janeiro hosts what is widely called the largest party on Earth — a five-day street and stadium carnival in which neighbourhood-based percussion-and-dance schools compete by parading along a purpose-built stadium-lined boulevard. What is the boulevard called?
context: The Sambodromo was designed by Oscar Niemeyer and opened 1984; it holds 70,000 spectators along a 700-metre runway. Each samba school's parade includes thousands of dancers, drummers, and elaborate floats following an annually chosen theme — judged on costumes, music, and theme execution.

question: In the rough dockside neighbourhoods of late-19th-century Buenos Aires, fused immigrant communities — Italian, Spanish, African Argentine, and rural gauchos — combined polka, habanera, and Andalusian musical traditions into a tightly embraced couple dance accompanied by an accordion-like instrument. What is this dance called?
context: The accordion-like instrument, the bandoneon, was actually a 19th-century German invention. Carlos Gardel — born in France, raised in Buenos Aires — became tango's first global star; his death in a plane crash in 1935 was mourned across South America.

question: An aristocratic cemetery in central Buenos Aires holds over 6,400 vaults and statues among tree-lined cobbled lanes. Eva Peron is buried here in her family's tomb (the famous Duarte vault, three locks deep against grave-robbing). Whose vaults make up the cemetery?
context: Eva Peron's body was stolen, hidden in Italy for 17 years after her 1952 death, and finally returned to the Duarte vault in 1976. Her tomb is reinforced against further grave-robbing. The cemetery covers 14 acres and is one of the most-visited tourist sites in the city.

question: In the middle of the Amazon rainforest, 1,500 km up the river, sits a flamboyant pink-and-cream Italianate opera house completed in 1896 — every paving stone, chandelier, and roof tile shipped up the Amazon, paid for with rubber-boom money. Caruso never sang there (he died first), but Pavarotti did. What city hosts it?
context: Manaus boomed from the late 19th-century rubber tap monopoly. The boom collapsed when British smugglers stole rubber seeds and planted them in Malaya; by 1920 the rubber economy had moved to Asia. The opera house decayed but was beautifully restored in the 1990s.

question: At the foot of the Andes in western Argentina sits a city built on the country's wine industry. Centuries-old earthquake-prone irrigation canals (the acequias) water vineyards at elevations between 600 and 1,500 metres, producing the country's signature deep, plummy red wine variety. What is this variety?
context: Malbec is originally from Cahors in southwest France, where it was nearly wiped out by phylloxera in the 19th century. French immigrants brought it to Argentina, where the high-altitude sunshine produces a much fruitier expression than the original French style.

question: On the Pacific coast of Chile sits a port city built on 42 steep coastal hills, with brightly painted ramshackle houses tumbling down cliffsides toward the harbour. To connect the upper barrios to the port, a network of antique funicular elevators (ascensores) has clattered up and down since the 1880s. About how many of these are still in service?
context: Several historic ascensores have been declared national monuments. The city was the most important port on the Pacific until the 1914 Panama Canal opened, then declined sharply. UNESCO recognised the historic centre in 2003.

question: On Bennelong Point in Sydney Harbour sits a 1973 building shaped like a series of soaring white shells — actually segments of a sphere of the same radius. The Danish architect was 38 when he won the international competition; the design was so unbuildable that the project ran 10 years late and 14 times over budget, and the architect resigned mid-project. Who designed it?
context: Utzon's geometric breakthrough — making each shell a segment of the same sphere — was found mid-project after years of trying other approaches. The opera house has 1,056,006 ceramic tiles in the shells; only Utzon's geometric insight made them buildable.

question: Melbourne's central business district hides a particular kind of attraction: narrow service alleys (originally for horse-and-cart deliveries) converted into small bars, cafes, and graffiti-art galleries. The city's coffee culture, dating to post-WWII Italian immigration, is intense — Melburnians take espresso seriously. What are these alleys generically called?
context: Hosier Lane is the most-photographed graffiti laneway; Degraves Street and Centre Place are bursting with cafe seating. Melbourne hosts the World Barista Championship regularly and has more cafes per capita than almost any city outside Italy.

question: Australia's federal capital was planned in 1913 by an American architect (Walter Burley Griffin) on undeveloped sheep-grazing land halfway between Sydney and Melbourne — both of which had refused to cede capital status to the other. The plan centres on an artificial lake and a triangle of monumental boulevards. What is the lake called?
context: Burley Griffin won the international competition with his wife Marion Mahony Griffin, who provided much of the famous draughtsmanship. The plan was largely abandoned during the World Wars and only partially executed; full lake-creation only happened in 1964 by damming the Molonglo River.

question: In the dry centre of Australia, the Anangu people consider a single 348-metre-tall sandstone monolith deeply sacred — a place of dreaming-time stories and ancestor songs. The rock's iron-bearing surface reddens at sunset and sunrise. Climbing it (a long-standing tourist tradition) was permanently banned in October 2019 at the Anangu's request. What is this rock called?
context: Uluru is about 9 km in circumference and extends an estimated 2.5 km underground — only about 10% is above the surface. UNESCO listed it as a Mixed cultural-natural property in 1987. Park rangers and tour operators support the climbing ban; tourism has continued to grow.

question: In the centre of New Zealand's North Island sits a town built atop one of the world's most active geothermal fields — bubbling mud pools, sulphurous gas vents, and over 700 active geothermal features in a 6,000-square-km caldera. The town is also a centre of Maori cultural tourism, hosting hangi feasts and traditional dance performances. What is the cultural performance called?
context: The famous haka — performed by the All Blacks before rugby matches — is one form of kapa haka. The traditional Rotorua haka is Ka Mate, composed by the chief Te Rauparaha around 1820. Local Maori iwi (tribes) operate many of the geothermal-zone tourism sites in the area.

question: About 3,500 km off the coast of Chile and 2,000 km from the nearest inhabited island, this small volcanic island holds about 900 monumental stone statues called moai — carved from volcanic tuff between roughly 1100 and 1600 AD by the indigenous Rapa Nui people. Most stand on stone platforms called ahu around the coast, facing inward. What is the island's Spanish-derived name?
context: Dutch admiral Jacob Roggeveen named the island in 1722 — he encountered it on Easter Sunday. The indigenous name is Rapa Nui. The island measures only 24 by 12 km. How the moai (up to 80 tons) were transported is now thought to involve a 'walking' rocking gait.

question: The largest French Polynesian city, on the north coast of the island of Tahiti, served as a major Pacific port and remains the administrative capital of the French overseas collectivity. Paul Gauguin painted his late masterpieces here. What is this city called?
context: Tahiti was annexed by France in 1880. Captain Cook observed the Transit of Venus from a beach east of modern Papeete in 1769. Gauguin lived in Tahiti and the Marquesas from 1891 to 1903; his last paintings — 'Where Do We Come From' (1897) — were done on Tahiti.

question: On the north coast of Upolu Island, Samoa's largest town hosts a colonial-era assembly building called Mulinu'u that was once the seat of indigenous government and is still used as a parliament. Robert Louis Stevenson, author of Treasure Island and Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde, spent his last years here and is buried on Mount Vaea above the town. What is this town called?
context: Stevenson moved to Samoa in 1890 for his health; he died there in 1894 at age 44. His house at Vailima is now a museum. The Samoan name for him was Tusitala ('teller of tales').

question: In central Croatia, sixteen turquoise lakes step down a steep wooded valley, separated by natural travertine dams that grow by about a centimetre per year as algae and bacteria deposit calcium carbonate. The barriers are constantly remade. What is this national park called?
context: Travertine dam growth is a natural ongoing process — the park's geology is alive. UNESCO listed Plitvice in 1979. Boardwalks weave between and across the lakes; wooden walkways replace each other as the travertine grows under them.

question: Swimming through the murky brown waters of the Amazon basin lives the world's largest freshwater dolphin — a species that has evolved to navigate flooded forest, with a long snout, flexible neck, and pink skin colouring (especially in mature males). What is it called?
context: The boto's flexibility — a real neck movement, unlike most dolphins — lets it slalom between flooded trees during the wet season. Amazonian river folklore says botos transform into beautiful men on full-moon nights and seduce village women — pregnancies are 'explained' this way.

question: The Nile flows about 6,650 km from its source near Lake Victoria in central Africa northward to the Mediterranean in Egypt — one of only a few major rivers in the world to flow north for most of its length. Where does the Blue Nile (which carries about 85% of the flow during the flood season) meet the White Nile?
context: The Blue Nile rises in Ethiopia at Lake Tana and the seasonal rains in the Ethiopian highlands create the Nile's annual flood. The White Nile is steadier; the Blue Nile is more variable. The Aswan High Dam (completed 1970) ended natural flooding downstream.

question: The Ganges rises in a Himalayan glacier in northern India and flows about 2,500 km to the Bay of Bengal, passing through some of the most religiously significant cities of Hinduism. Bathing in it is considered to purify the soul; ashes of the dead are scattered in it. At which glacier-cave does the river officially begin?
context: Gaumukh is the snout of the Gangotri Glacier at about 4,000 metres elevation. The cave-shaped opening receding glacier looks like a cow's mouth — the local name. The glacier is retreating, so the source point has been moving upstream over decades.

question: The lower Mississippi between Cairo (Illinois) and the Gulf of Mexico carves wide bends through soft alluvial sediment, sometimes cutting through its own neck to leave a curved abandoned channel behind. These crescent-shaped abandoned channels survive as lakes. What are they called?
context: The Mississippi has shifted its main channel several times in geological history — and once major events can move it again. The 1927 flood, the worst U.S. flood disaster ever, dramatically reshaped the lower Mississippi's path and changed the federal flood-control system.

question: The River Thames, which flows through London, is tidal up to Teddington (88 km from the sea); twice a day the sea-tide pushes upstream, raising the water level in central London by about 7 metres. The Thames Barrier (a series of moveable steel gates near Woolwich) has protected the city from flood surges since 1982. What is the smaller tidal-bore wave the Thames produces?
answer: A modest bore called the Aegir
choices: A modest bore called the Aegir
context: Tidal bores happen when an incoming tide funnels into a narrow shallow estuary. The Severn bore (5 metres tall) on the river of that name is the biggest in Britain; the Thames bore is mild but real. The Thames Barrier is closed about 6-10 times a year on average.

question: The Indus River — main river of Pakistan and ancient cradle of the Indus Valley Civilisation — hosts a critically endangered blind freshwater dolphin that navigates the river's muddy water by sonar. Side-swimming (lying on its side as it moves) is a distinctive feature. About how many remain in the wild?
context: The bhulan, the local name, was once distributed throughout the Indus and its main tributaries. Construction of dams has fragmented its range; conservation programs in Sindh province have stabilised the population. The Chinese baiji (Yangtze) of the same lineage was declared functionally extinct in 2006.

question: Lake Baikal in Siberia hosts the only fully freshwater seal species in the world — about 70,000 individuals, possibly trapped in the lake when Siberian glaciation isolated it from the Arctic Ocean millions of years ago. What is this seal called?
context: Two other freshwater seals exist — the Caspian and the Lake Ladoga ringed seal — but both have brackish or partly saline ancestry. The Baikal nerpa is the only fully freshwater species. How its ancestors reached the lake remains a mystery; one theory is via the Yenisei river system.

question: On the border of four central African countries — Chad, Niger, Nigeria, and Cameroon — once stretched one of the largest freshwater lakes in Africa. Since the 1960s, irrigation, drought, and climate change have reduced it by what percentage?
context: Lake Chad sits in an endorheic basin — the water has no outlet to the sea. The drying has accelerated since the 1960s; the southern part remains relatively stable, but the northern part has nearly disappeared. The Lake Chad Basin Commission coordinates regional management.

question: In southern Oregon sits the deepest lake in the United States — 594 metres — filling a caldera that formed about 7,700 years ago when Mount Mazama collapsed in one of the largest volcanic eruptions of the Holocene. The lake water is so pure and deep blue that visibility extends down to 40 metres. What is the lake called?
context: Mazama's eruption ejected about 50 cubic km of material — about 100 times larger than Mount St Helens 1980. The lake takes about 250 years to refill via precipitation and snowmelt. Wizard Island, a small cinder cone, juts from the lake's surface — a post-collapse mini-volcano.

question: Off Western Australia's southern coast on Middle Island sits a small lake permanently a bright cotton-candy pink. The colour comes from microbial life adapted to the salty water — halophilic bacteria and microalgae. Other places (Senegal, Mexico, Spain) also have pink lakes; this Western Australian one was first noted by which 19th-century European explorer?
context: Lake Hillier is about 600 m by 250 m. Algae of the genus Dunaliella salina and bacteria of the genus Halobacterium produce carotenoid pigments. Lake Retba in Senegal and Las Coloradas in Yucatan are similarly pink — same biological mechanism.

question: On the border of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, a deep Rift Valley lake holds something dangerous beneath its calm surface: about 65 cubic km of dissolved methane and 250 cubic km of carbon dioxide. If a volcanic eruption or earthquake disturbed it, the gas could erupt — as has happened at smaller crater lakes nearby. What lake is this?
context: Lake Nyos in Cameroon erupted in 1986, killing 1,700 people in the valley below from CO2 asphyxiation. Kivu is much larger; a similar event could kill millions. Rwanda has begun extracting the methane for power generation, which also reduces the risk.

question: Across Mexico's Yucatan peninsula, thousands of natural sinkholes connect to a vast underground river system in the limestone bedrock. The Maya considered them entrances to the underworld and offered ritual goods (and sometimes humans) at them. What are these sinkholes called?
context: The Chicxulub impact crater 65 million years ago shattered the Yucatan bedrock; the cenote network roughly follows the ring of the impact basin. The Sac Actun cave system, partly submerged, runs over 350 km and is the longest underwater cave system in the world.

question: The highest peak in North America rises 6,190 metres in interior Alaska. Originally known by the Koyukon Athabascan name meaning 'the high one', it was officially named Mount McKinley by Congress in 1917 over local objection, and was renamed back by federal order in 2015. What is its name today?
context: Denali is the steepest mountain on Earth from base to peak — its base sits at about 600 metres elevation, giving a vertical relief of about 5,500 metres. Everest's base camp sits at 5,300 metres, so its base-to-summit relief is only about 3,500 metres.

question: On Japan's main island of Honshu, an almost perfectly symmetrical volcanic cone rises 3,776 metres — the highest peak in Japan, last erupted in 1707-1708 (the Hoei eruption). The mountain is sacred in Shinto and is the country's most-painted, most-photographed natural symbol. What is it called?
context: Fuji is a stratovolcano formed from three overlapping volcanoes. About 300,000 people climb it during the official July-September climbing season. The Hoei eruption blew a side crater (Hoeizan) into the cone's east flank — visible from below. UNESCO World Heritage 2013 as a cultural rather than natural site.

question: The Himalayas — which contain all 14 of the world's mountains over 8,000 metres — were formed (and are still forming) by which tectonic event?
answer: The Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate (started ~50 million years ago)
choices: The Indian Plate colliding with the Eurasian Plate (started ~50 million years ago)
The Pacific Plate subducting beneath the Eurasian Plate
Volcanic activity along a divergent hotspot in northern India
Ancient glaciation eroding a Tibetan plateau to leave high ridges
context: The Indian plate was a separate continent attached to Antarctica until about 130 million years ago, when it broke off and drifted north at unusually high speed (15 cm per year). It collided with Asia around 50 million years ago; the leading edge of India is still being driven northward, pushing Tibet up.

question: Stretching across Botswana, Namibia, and South Africa, this red-sand 'thirstland' is technically a semi-desert — it gets 5-25 cm of rain a year, enough for grass and acacia trees in places. The indigenous San (Bushmen) have lived here as hunter-gatherers for tens of thousands of years. What is the desert called?
context: Okavango Delta, in northern Botswana, is a vast inland wetland where the Okavango River disappears into the Kalahari sands. The San speak languages with click consonants — among the oldest language families on Earth. The 1980 film 'The Gods Must Be Crazy' was filmed in the Kalahari.

question: At 5,000 metres in the Chilean Atacama Desert sits one of the most advanced ground-based astronomical facilities on Earth — 66 radio dish antennas (12 metres each) on a moveable platform, observing at millimetre wavelengths to peer through dust clouds and detect distant galaxies and forming stars. What is it called?
context: ALMA went into full operation in 2013. The dry, high site is crucial: water vapour in air absorbs millimetre-wavelength light, so the higher and drier, the better. The instruments are too sensitive to be operated by humans nearby — staff control them from a base camp 30 km lower.
