question: Spanning parts of Arizona, California, and northwestern Mexico, this desert has the highest plant and animal diversity of any North American desert — including a unique columnar cactus (Carnegiea gigantea) that grows up to 12 metres and lives 150-200 years. What is the cactus called?
context: Saguaros do not grow their first 'arms' until about age 75. They produce night-blooming white flowers (Arizona's state flower) pollinated by lesser long-nosed bats. The species is protected — destroying or moving one in Arizona is a felony.

question: Antarctica is technically a desert — it receives less than 200 mm of precipitation per year (mostly as snow that accumulates rather than melting). It is the largest desert on Earth — about 14 million square kilometres. What is the average annual precipitation at the South Pole itself?
context: The South Pole gets perhaps 50-80 mm of snow per year, which compacts to under 10 mm water equivalent. The continent's coastal margins get more snow. The Atacama is the driest non-polar desert; the Antarctic Dry Valleys (no ice cover) are arguably the driest place on Earth — no rain in millions of years in some spots.

question: Greenland is the world's largest island that is not a continent, and over 80% of its surface is covered by an ice sheet up to how thick at its centre?
context: The Greenland ice sheet has been there for at least 1 million years. Recent melting has accelerated — the sheet is losing about 280 billion tons of ice per year on average. If completely melted, global sea level would rise about 7 metres.

question: Above the Earth's polar regions, charged particles from the Sun stream along the magnetic-field lines into the upper atmosphere, where they collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms and excite them to glow in greens, pinks, reds, and violets. What is the northern version of this phenomenon called?
context: Green is the most common colour: oxygen at about 100 km altitude. Red comes from oxygen at very high altitude (200-300 km). Purple/pink comes from nitrogen. Aurora is most visible between geomagnetic latitudes 60-75. The solar maximum (every 11 years) increases aurora frequency.

question: Across the high Arctic — Siberia, Alaska, northern Canada — soil that has remained frozen for at least two years (often for thousands) is called permafrost. As it thaws, it releases what greenhouse gas trapped in ancient organic matter?
context: Permafrost holds an estimated 1,500 gigatons of carbon — roughly twice what is in the atmosphere currently. As it thaws, microbial decomposition releases CO2 in oxygen-rich conditions and methane in waterlogged conditions. Both are major climate-feedback concerns.

question: In southern Argentine Patagonia, a 5-km-wide tongue of ice descends from the Southern Patagonian Ice Field to Lake Argentino, periodically blocking the lake. Pressure builds; eventually a spectacular dam break occurs as ice collapses into the lake — a tourist event that draws huge crowds. What is this glacier called?
context: Perito Moreno is one of the few major glaciers in the world not retreating significantly — its terminus is roughly stable. The dam-rupture event has happened 23 times since 1947, sometimes more than a decade apart. Most other Patagonian ice-field glaciers are retreating rapidly.

question: Africa's largest contiguous rainforest covers about 200 million hectares across six countries — Cameroon, Central African Republic, Republic of the Congo, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Equatorial Guinea, and Gabon. What is its informal name?
context: The Congo Basin's forests are second only to the Amazon in area and biodiversity. The basin holds about 30 million people. Forest elephants (a smaller distinct species from savanna elephants), forest buffalo, gorillas, chimpanzees, bonobos, and okapi all live here.

question: Along the foggy northern California coast grow the tallest trees on Earth — coastal redwoods (Sequoia sempervirens) up to 115 metres tall. Their height limit is set largely by the difficulty of pulling water that far up against gravity. The tallest known living individual is called what?
context: Hyperion's exact location is kept secret to protect it from tourists. The redwoods have only one close relative, the dawn redwood (Metasequoia, native to a small area of China). Coastal redwoods need the marine fog that drips onto their canopies for hydration.

question: In the dry White Mountains and Inyo National Forest of California grow the oldest non-clonal organisms on Earth — twisted, half-dead-looking pines whose oldest living individual is over 4,800 years old. What species is this?
context: The oldest documented bristlecone — Methuselah — germinated about 2832 BC. Its exact location is kept secret. The trees grow only millimetres a year, in very dense, resinous wood that resists decay. A still-older tree (5,062 years in 2017) was found nearby but its location and identifier have not been disclosed.

question: In Utah's Fishlake National Forest, a clonal stand of quaking aspen — all genetically identical, all interconnected by a single root system — covers 43 hectares with about 47,000 stems. By total mass, this single organism may be the largest on Earth. What is it called?
context: Pando is estimated at 14,000 to 80,000 years old depending on method. Stems above ground rarely live more than 150 years; the root system is what carries the genetic identity. Recent studies show Pando is in decline — overgrazing by deer that no longer fear extinct wolves keeps new shoots from surviving.

question: A warm-water current carries heat from the Gulf of Mexico across the North Atlantic, helping keep northwestern Europe far warmer than its latitude alone would suggest — London at 51° N is much milder than Calgary at 51° N. What is this current called?
context: The Gulf Stream is about 100 km wide and transports more water than all the rivers on Earth combined. Climate change projections include possible weakening of the AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) that drives it; a major shutdown would be disastrous for European climate.

question: The Black Sea is unusual among Earth's seas: below about 200 metres depth, its water is essentially devoid of oxygen — anoxic, due to limited circulation with the Mediterranean through the Bosphorus and high freshwater inflow. What practical effect does this have on shipwrecks below 200 metres?
answer: Wooden hulls and organic materials are exceptionally well preserved
choices: Wooden hulls and organic materials are exceptionally well preserved
Wooden hulls dissolve much faster than in oxygenated water
Metals corrode much faster due to sulfide chemistry
Anoxic water is biologically active and consumes wood
context: The Black Sea Maritime Archaeology Project has discovered Byzantine, Roman, Greek, and Ottoman ships at depths down to 2 km, with intact wood, rigging, and even fragments of cargo. The anoxic Black Sea is one of the world's most important time capsules for ancient maritime history.

question: In northern Arizona, the Colorado River has cut through 2 billion years of geological history into the Colorado Plateau, exposing rock layers from the Vishnu Schist (1.8 billion years old) at the bottom to the Kaibab Limestone at the top. About how many million years has this carving taken?
context: The canyon is about 446 km long, up to 29 km wide, and 1.8 km deep at its deepest. The relatively rapid carving — geologically speaking — was made possible by the plateau being uplifted while the river course was already in place, forcing the river to cut down as the land rose.

question: In southwestern Utah, an amphitheatre of pink-orange rock holds the densest concentration of tall thin spires anywhere on Earth — thousands of them, formed by frost wedging and water erosion. What are these spires called?
context: Bryce Canyon's hoodoos form in the Claron Formation — soft limestone capped by harder rock that resists weathering. The cap-rock protects a narrow tower beneath until eventually weathering tips it. Paiute legend says the hoodoos are people turned to stone by a trickster god.

question: In southeastern Utah and northeastern Arizona, on Navajo Nation land, isolated sandstone monoliths rise as much as 300 metres straight up from a flat desert floor. The site became one of the world's most photographed landscapes after John Ford filmed John Wayne westerns here. What are the monoliths called?
context: The visible monoliths are remnants of a once-continuous Permian sandstone plateau that has eroded around them. The Navajo (Dine) name is Tse'Bii'Ndzisgaii. Visitors enter via the Monument Valley Navajo Tribal Park; the iconic 'Mittens' and Merrick Butte appear in countless westerns.

question: In central Anatolia, Turkey, volcanic ash from ancient eruptions of Mount Erciyes hardened into soft tuff that erosion has carved into spires sometimes capped by harder volcanic rock — creating thousands of tall, hat-topped pillars. Early Christians dug churches and even whole underground cities into the soft rock. What is the region called?
context: Beneath Cappadocia lies the Derinkuyu underground city — at least 11 levels deep, capacity for 20,000 people, with stables, churches, kitchens, and ventilation shafts. It was used by Christians fleeing Roman and later Muslim persecution. The fairy chimneys' caps are basalt; the pillars are tuff.

question: In western Turkey, hot mineral springs flowing down a hillside have deposited terraces of brilliant white travertine over millennia, creating a 'cotton castle' visible from kilometres away. The ancient Roman city of Hierapolis was built on top. What is the natural site called?
context: The terraced pools cascade for 2.7 km. The waters are about 35-100°C at the springs. UNESCO listed Pamukkale-Hierapolis as a Mixed Site in 1988. Tourist damage in the 1990s led to flow restrictions; some terraces were partly drying up.

question: In Yellowstone National Park, the largest hot spring in the United States — 110 metres across, deeper than a six-storey building — circles concentric rings of brilliant blue, green, yellow, orange, and red. The colours come from heat-loving microorganisms forming different bands at different water temperatures. What is the spring called?
context: The blue centre is sterile (too hot for microbes, about 87°C). Cyanobacteria and other thermophiles thrive at progressively cooler temperatures, each species producing different carotenoid pigments. The orange ring is dominated by Synechococcus elongatus; the green by chlorophyll-producing thermophiles.

question: Yellowstone's most famous geyser erupts every 60-110 minutes (interval varying after the 1959 Hebgen Lake earthquake), shooting boiling water 30-55 metres into the air for about 3 minutes. What is the geyser called?
context: Old Faithful is not the largest or the most regular geyser, but it is the most predictably regular major geyser. Steamboat (also in Yellowstone) is the tallest geyser on Earth when it does erupt — up to 110 metres — but it can go years between eruptions. About 300 of the 500 active geysers on Earth are in Yellowstone.

question: Occasionally at sunset over the ocean, the last sliver of the setting sun appears for a fraction of a second as brilliant green before disappearing. The effect is caused by Earth's atmosphere acting as a prism, refracting the shorter wavelengths more. What is this phenomenon called?
context: The green flash requires a clear horizon and very stable atmospheric conditions. Sailors and pilots have reported it for centuries; Jules Verne wrote a romantic novel about it in 1882. Captured on video most reliably at high mountain summits looking down on a flat horizon.

question: Every 2-7 years, a band of warm Pacific water spreads eastward toward South America, suppressing the cold Humboldt upwelling and disrupting weather across the planet. The effect was first noticed by Peruvian fishermen who named it after the Christ child because it usually peaked around Christmas. What is it called?
context: El Nino changes rainfall around the Pacific Rim — drought in Australia and Indonesia, floods in Peru and Ecuador, a milder hurricane season in the Atlantic, more storms in the eastern Pacific. La Nina is the opposite phase — anomalously cold east Pacific.

question: Between latitudes 40°S and 50°S in the Southern Hemisphere, westerly winds blow uninterrupted around the globe with no continents to slow them. Mariners on the clipper-ship route from Europe to Australia took advantage of these winds; they also drive the Antarctic Circumpolar Current. What are they called?
context: The names extend with latitude: the 50s are 'Furious', the 60s are 'Screaming'. The Southern Ocean has no land between South Africa, Australia, and South America at this latitude, so wind builds up with nothing to break it. Clippers loaded with wool ran 'east-about' around the globe.

question: Between the Rocky Mountains and the Mississippi River in central North America, cold dry air from Canada repeatedly meets warm humid air from the Gulf of Mexico, producing the densest cluster of tornadoes on Earth. About how many tornadoes hit the United States in an average year?
context: Tornado Alley typically covers Texas, Oklahoma, Kansas, Nebraska, and parts of South Dakota. The most destructive tornadoes (EF5) are concentrated here. The U.S. has more tornadoes than any other country in the world; Bangladesh and Argentina also have substantial activity.

question: Each winter from late November to mid-March, a dry, dust-laden wind blows from the Sahara southwest across West Africa, dropping humidity to single-digit percentages and dimming the sun. What is this wind called?
context: The Harmattan dust can reach as far as the Caribbean — actually fertilising the Amazon basin with mineral-rich Saharan dust that has crossed the Atlantic. The wind dries skin and lips painfully; the haze is sometimes thick enough to ground flights.

question: In the spring (typically April-June), a hot dry sand-laden wind from the Sahara sweeps over Egypt for about fifty days, lifting temperatures by 20°C, scouring crops, and reducing visibility. The wind is named for its duration. What is it called in Arabic?
context: The Khamsin can blow for several days in a row at gale strength. It is the same kind of wind as the Sirocco in Italy and the Sharav in Israel; the name is regional. Egyptian farmers historically considered the Khamsin a major threat to spring harvests.

question: About 1,000 km off Ecuador's coast in the Pacific lie volcanic islands where Darwin spent five weeks in 1835 observing the unique wildlife — finches with diverse beak shapes, marine and land iguanas, giant tortoises, flightless cormorants. What is this archipelago called?
context: The islands sit on a hotspot like Hawaii — each volcanic island ages as the Nazca plate carries it eastward away from the source. Darwin's observations contributed to On the Origin of Species (1859); the finches' adaptive radiation has been further studied by Peter and Rosemary Grant since the 1970s.

question: On a handful of small Indonesian islands lives the largest lizard on Earth — about 3 metres long, 90 kg, with a venomous bite and a willingness to ambush water buffaloes, deer, and occasionally humans. About how many remain in the wild?
context: Komodo dragons live on Komodo, Rinca, Padar, Flores, and Gili Motang in the Lesser Sundas. They survived on these isolated islands; mainland Australian relatives went extinct in the Holocene. They are now the largest predators of Komodo National Park.

question: In northern Botswana, the Okavango River — which flows about 1,600 km from the Angolan highlands — never reaches the sea. Instead it spreads out over the Kalahari sands in a vast seasonal wetland of channels, papyrus swamps, and 'islands' (some are anthills). Elephants, lions, leopards, and hippos all live here. What kind of geographic feature is this?
context: The Okavango Delta is one of the few major endorheic deltas on Earth (water has no outlet to sea). The annual flood pulse drives ecological activity — wildlife congregates in dry season around the persistent channels. UNESCO Natural World Heritage Site since 2014.

question: About 252 million years ago, the largest known volcanic eruption sequence in Earth's history covered some 7 million square kilometres of Siberia in basaltic lava over about 1-2 million years. The CO2 release drove climate change that caused the Permian-Triassic mass extinction — Earth's worst — killing about 96% of marine species. What is this lava province called?
context: 'Traps' is from the Swedish 'trappa' (stair) referring to the stepped landscape of the eroded basalt flows. The Siberian Traps eruption injected so much CO2 and sulfur into the atmosphere that ocean acidification, anoxia, and global warming all contributed to the extinction.

question: In Kentucky stretches the world's longest cave system — over 686 km of surveyed passages on multiple levels, with new sections still being discovered. The cave formed in limestone, partly capped by a layer of insoluble sandstone that protected the bedrock from collapse. What is this cave system called?
context: Mammoth Cave's history of human use goes back 4,000 years. Native Americans mined gypsum and crystals from it. UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1981. The cave is roughly twice as long as the second-longest known system (Sistema Sac Actun in Mexico, mostly underwater).

question: Polynesian navigators settled the most remote islands on Earth — from Hawaii to Easter Island to New Zealand — between about 1000 BC and 1300 AD, sailing without maps, charts, sextants, or compasses. What suite of observational techniques did they use?
answer: Star compass, wave patterns, cloud signs, bird flight
choices: Star compass, wave patterns, cloud signs, bird flight
Solar elevation tables and lead-line soundings
Latitude beads carved on whale tooth implements
context: Mau Piailug of Satawal taught the lost art of Pacific wayfinding to Nainoa Thompson of the Hokule'a — a replica voyaging canoe sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti in 1976 using only traditional methods. The voyage proved that systematic deliberate navigation, not chance drift, settled the Pacific.

question: Inside the Great Temple of Amun at Karnak (modern Luxor) stretches the largest temple hall ever built — about 50 metres deep, 100 metres wide, supported by 134 sandstone columns up to 21 metres tall. Originally painted in vivid blues, reds, and yellows; reliefs cover every visible surface. What is this kind of column-filled hall called?
context: Pharaohs Seti I and Ramesses II built most of the hall (around 1300-1280 BC). The central nave's tallest columns are larger than the supporting outer ranks; the height difference let clerestory windows admit light, dimly filtering down to the floor below. The columns are papyrus-bud and papyrus-flower shaped — a stone forest of the Nile marsh.

question: Founded by Darius the Great around 515 BC in southern Iran, the ceremonial capital of the Persian Achaemenid Empire featured a vast audience hall (the Apadana) reached by long stairs whose carved reliefs depict envoys from 23 subject nations bringing tribute. Each envoy is shown in his own national dress. What kind of stone are the reliefs carved into?
answer: Limestone (grey limestone of the local quarries)
choices: Limestone (grey limestone of the local quarries)
context: Alexander the Great burned Persepolis in 330 BC; whether as a deliberate revenge for Xerxes' burning of Athens or in a drunken party is debated. The relief programme — about 3,000 figures — survives because limestone resists weathering in the dry climate. UNESCO World Heritage 1979.

question: The eighth gate to the inner city of ancient Babylon was built around 575 BC under Nebuchadnezzar II — its surface entirely covered in glazed blue bricks with relief figures of dragons (mushhushshu) and bulls. The gate was excavated by German archaeologists in 1902-1914 and reassembled in a museum. Where does it stand today?
context: Only the smaller front section was reconstructed in Berlin; the rest sits in storage. A reproduction stands at the original Babylon site in Iraq. Iraq has periodically demanded the return of the gate; Germany has not complied. The Ishtar Gate's blue is from glazes coloured by ground lapis lazuli.

question: On the Aegean coast of Anatolia (modern Bergama, Turkey), a great altar to Zeus was built around 175 BC by the Pergamene kingdom. Its monumental friezes depict the Gigantomachy — the battle between gods and giants — in some of the most dynamic Hellenistic sculpture ever carved. Where is the main altar today?
context: Sourced as part of late-19th-century German excavations and shipped to Berlin between 1879 and 1886. Turkey periodically requests its return. The Gigantomachy frieze is about 113 metres long — one of the longest surviving sculptural narratives from antiquity.

question: At Ephesus in western Anatolia, a Roman library facade — twin storeys of paired columns and four statue niches representing wisdom, knowledge, intelligence, and virtue — has been reconstructed from the ruins. Once it held about 12,000 scrolls. After whom was the library named?
context: Celsus was the Roman governor of Asia province in 105-107 AD. His son Aquila built the library in his honour around 135 AD; Celsus is buried in a sarcophagus beneath it. The facade is one of the most photographed sites in Turkey; it was reconstructed by Austrian archaeologists in the 1970s.

question: On 24 August 79 AD (or possibly 24 October — the date is disputed), Mount Vesuvius in Italy erupted, burying the Roman city of Pompeii under about 6 metres of ash and pumice within 24 hours. Many residents who tried to flee were killed by what kind of volcanic phenomenon?
context: Pliny the Younger, who watched from across the bay, described the eruption in two letters to Tacitus. The pyroclastic flows that killed people in Pompeii reached temperatures of 250-300°C and travelled hundreds of km/h. The volcanic ash perfectly preserved buildings, frescoes, and even the shapes of bodies (made into plaster casts by Giuseppe Fiorelli).

question: About 15 km from Pompeii, the nearby coastal city of Herculaneum was buried even more deeply — under about 20 metres of pyroclastic material that quickly hardened. The high temperature carbonised organic materials: wooden furniture, food in pots, papyrus scrolls. Where was a unique library of carbonised philosophical scrolls found?
context: About 1,800 scrolls were found in the Villa of the Papyri in 1750 — mostly Epicurean philosophy by Philodemus. They are blackened and fragile. Recent X-ray and AI techniques are letting researchers read them without unrolling them — the 'Vesuvius Challenge' competition has produced the first readable text from sealed scrolls.

question: The Flavian Amphitheatre — the Colosseum of Rome, completed in 80 AD under Emperor Titus — could seat about 50,000-80,000 spectators on multiple levels. The arena floor had to accommodate gladiator combat, animal hunts, and even mock naval battles. What was the system of underground corridors and lifts beneath the arena called?
context: The hypogeum is a two-level basement with 32 animal cages, 80 vertical lifts, and trapdoors that brought up gladiators, animals, and scenery on cue. The arena floor itself was wooden over the hypogeum. The vomitoria were the broad passages through which spectators (vomere = to spew out) entered and exited.

question: The Pantheon in Rome, completed around 126 AD under Emperor Hadrian, still holds a record: it has the world's largest unreinforced concrete dome — 43 metres across. Roman concrete used lightweight aggregates (pumice, scoria) at the top of the dome and heavier ones at the base. What ancient binder made the concrete so durable?
choices: Volcanic lava blocks bonded with bitumen
context: Pozzolana ash from Pozzuoli (near Naples) reacts with lime and seawater to produce calcium-aluminium-silicate-hydrate (CASH) crystals that grow and strengthen the concrete over centuries. Modern Portland cement does not have this self-healing property; engineers are now studying Roman concrete to learn its long-term strength.

question: The 6th-century Hagia Sophia in Constantinople (modern Istanbul) was the largest interior space in the world for centuries. Its 32-metre-diameter dome rises 56 metres above the floor; rectangular windows at its base let in light. What architectural element allowed the round dome to sit on a square base?
context: Pendentives spread the dome's weight onto four corner piers. Architects Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus invented (or perfected) the technique. The original dome collapsed in 558; a higher and more stable rebuild was completed by 562. The technique then spread across Byzantine and Islamic architecture.

question: In northern Cambodia, the 12th-century temple complex of Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument by area on Earth — about 162 hectares (1.6 sq km). Originally dedicated to Vishnu under the Khmer king Suryavarman II (around 1113-1150), the temple later became Buddhist. What is unusual about the temple's orientation?
answer: It faces west — unusual for a Hindu temple, which usually face east
choices: It faces west — unusual for a Hindu temple, which usually face east
It faces south — unusual for any temple in northern hemisphere
It faces directly toward Mount Kailash in Tibet
It faces directly toward the rising Sirius on the summer solstice
context: West-facing temples are usually associated with funerary use; some scholars think Angkor Wat may have served partly as Suryavarman's mausoleum. The complex appears on the Cambodian flag, the only national flag to feature a building.

question: About 50 km east of Borobudur on Java stand the tallest Hindu temples in Southeast Asia — three central towers (dedicated to Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva) rising up to 47 metres, surrounded by 224 smaller temples. The complex was built in the mid-9th century, perhaps as a Hindu response to nearby Buddhist Borobudur. What is it called?
context: Many of the surrounding smaller temples were destroyed by earthquakes — the 2006 Yogyakarta quake also damaged Prambanan. Restoration is ongoing. A Ramayana ballet is performed on its outdoor stages under the full moon during the dry season.

question: In Sri Lanka's medieval capital (12th century), four colossal granite Buddha images carved directly into a single rock face are some of the finest Buddhist sculpture anywhere — a 7-metre reclining Buddha (entering Parinirvana), a standing 7-metre Buddha, and two seated meditation figures. What is this site called?
context: Polonnaruwa was the medieval Sri Lankan capital after the abandonment of Anuradhapura. The Gal Vihara reliefs were carved under King Parakramabahu the Great in the 12th century. The standing figure's identity is debated — most scholars now consider it the disciple Ananda or perhaps the Buddha in mourning.

question: On India's southeastern (Coromandel) coast stands a group of 7th-8th-century Pallava-dynasty temples carved partly from living rock — five rathas (chariot-temples), a giant bas-relief called 'Descent of the Ganges', and the seaside Shore Temple itself. What is the modern town's name?
context: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami briefly exposed older underwater ruins offshore, confirming legends of seven coastal temples now largely submerged. The 'Descent of the Ganges' bas-relief is the largest open-air bas-relief in the world — 27 metres long, 9 metres tall, depicting elephants, gods, and ascetics.

question: In central India sit a group of 10th-11th-century Hindu and Jain temples (about 25 survive of an original 85) covered in carvings of dancers, deities, scenes of daily life — and a small but famous set of explicit erotic carvings interpreted variously as tantric, allegorical, or decorative. The temples were built by which dynasty?
context: Khajuraho was abandoned around 1335 and forgotten in jungle until a British engineer rediscovered it in 1838. The erotic sculptures form only about 10% of the total carvings but draw the most attention. The temples are aligned for astronomical events; some scholars argue the erotic figures are protective amulets against the evil eye.

question: In south-central India, scattered across a 25-sq-km granite-boulder landscape, sit the ruins of the medieval Hindu Vijayanagara Empire's capital — temples, palaces, royal stables, public markets, sluice gates and water tanks. The empire fell after a 1565 battle. After whose 5,400 boulder-strewn hills is the area called?
context: Vijayanagara was probably the second-largest city in the world (after Beijing) around 1500, with perhaps 500,000 residents. The 1565 Battle of Talikota destroyed the empire; the city was looted and burned for six months by the victorious Deccan sultanates. UNESCO World Heritage 1986.

question: In western India, a horseshoe-shaped cliff above the Waghora river is pierced by 30 Buddhist rock-cut caves with elaborate murals from the 2nd century BC to the 5th century AD. The paintings depict the Buddha's previous lives (Jataka tales) in narrative style. When were the caves rediscovered?
context: John Smith was hunting tigers when he saw the openings in the cliff. The murals had survived because abandoned monasteries hidden behind monsoon-jungle were not disturbed. Their pigment chemistry, technique, and complete narrative scope make them one of Asia's most important cultural sites. UNESCO 1983.

question: Akbar's planned city near Agra, completed in 1585 in red sandstone, was abandoned by 1610 — most likely because what natural resource ran out?
answer: Water — the artificial lake supplying the city dried up
choices: Water — the artificial lake supplying the city dried up
Wood for cooking fuel — the surrounding forests were over-cut
Marble for ongoing construction — the Makrana quarries closed
Manpower — plague killed thousands of inhabitants
context: The Fatehpur Sikri lake was created by damming the Bharatpur stream; it silted up and ran low. Akbar moved to Lahore in 1585, then back to Agra. The city remained mostly intact because it was abandoned rather than destroyed — preserved as a near-perfect Mughal time capsule.

question: In 1974 farmers in Lintong (near Xi'an, China) digging a well uncovered the first of what proved to be a vast underground complex of life-size pottery soldiers — perhaps 8,000 in total, each with individually modelled faces, originally painted, organised in battle formation to guard the tomb of the first emperor of unified China. Who was this emperor?
context: Qin Shi Huang unified China in 221 BC and died in 210 BC; the burial took 38 years and engaged perhaps 700,000 workers. His own tomb mound has not been opened; ancient texts describe rivers of mercury flowing in it, and soil samples confirm extremely high mercury levels. Excavation awaits methods to preserve the originally bright paint, which fades within minutes of air exposure.

question: The defensive walls along China's northern frontier, built and rebuilt by successive dynasties from the 7th century BC to the 17th century AD, total a remarkable length. A 2012 official survey gave a total length including branches and reconstructions. What did the survey find?
context: The 21,196 km figure includes all dynasties' walls including branches, parallel walls, and overlapping rebuilds. The Ming-dynasty 'main wall' is about 8,850 km — the bricks-and-stone wall most familiar to tourists. The Great Wall is not visible from space with the naked eye — a common claim disproven by Chinese astronaut Yang Liwei in 2003.

question: Inside Beijing's old city sat the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing dynasties from 1420 to 1912 — about 980 buildings on 72 hectares enclosed by an 8-metre wall and 52-metre moat. The yellow glazed roof tiles signal imperial use; only the emperor's family and approved officials could enter. What is its Chinese name?
context: 'Purple' refers to the polestar constellation, considered the celestial home of the celestial emperor. The Forbidden City was the largest palace complex on Earth. Many of its treasures were moved to Taipei in 1948-49 during the Chinese Civil War; both palace museums hold significant Qing collections.

question: Near Nara, Japan, stands the oldest surviving wooden structure in the world — a Buddhist temple complex founded around 607 AD by Prince Shotoku. The main hall (Kondo) and five-storey pagoda are largely original 7th-century construction. What is the temple called?
context: Horyu-ji's pagoda contains a central pillar made from a tree felled around 594 AD. Earthquakes have shaken Japan repeatedly for fourteen centuries; the pagoda survives because each of its five storeys is independently flexible — the building sways but does not crack. UNESCO World Heritage 1993.

question: Discovered in 1994 in southeastern Turkey, this hilltop sanctuary has rewritten the early history of religion: T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 metres tall, carved with animal reliefs (boars, vultures, lions, snakes), arranged in circles, all dating to about 9500 BC — built by pre-pottery, pre-agricultural hunter-gatherers. What is the site called?
context: Gobekli Tepe predates Stonehenge by 6,000 years and the pyramids by 7,000 years. It was deliberately buried by its builders around 8000 BC — an enigma scholars still puzzle over. The site challenges the long-held idea that monumental religion requires settled agricultural societies.

question: In the Indus Valley of what is now Pakistan, a 2600-1900 BC city had paved streets in a precise north-south, east-west grid; nearly every house had a private bathroom with terracotta pipes draining to a city-wide covered sewer system — an urban water management more advanced than anywhere else in the world at the time. What is the city called?
context: Mohenjo-daro means 'Mound of the Dead' in Sindhi. Excavations began in 1922. The Indus Valley script remains undeciphered; we do not know what the inhabitants called themselves or their language. The civilisation declined and disappeared around 1900 BC for reasons still debated — climate change, river shifts, and migration are all candidates.

question: About 50 km northeast of Mexico City, a vast pre-Columbian city built around 100 BC-650 AD contains the third-largest pyramid in the world (by volume) — 75 metres tall, built over a sacred cave. The city's population may have reached 200,000 — among the largest in the ancient Americas. What is the pyramid called?
context: Teotihuacan ('place where gods were born' in Nahuatl) was already a ruin when the Aztecs encountered it. The Aztecs gave its monuments the names we use; we do not know what the original builders called themselves or their city. Excavations under the Pyramid of the Sun reveal a four-chamber natural cave with pre-pyramid offerings.

question: In the rainforest of Chiapas, Mexico, a 7th-8th-century Mayan city contains an elaborate temple-pyramid whose hidden internal staircase descends to a stone-lined royal tomb. The 5-ton stone slab covering the sarcophagus depicts the deceased king falling into the underworld — sometimes wildly reinterpreted as 'a Mayan astronaut'. Whose tomb is it?
context: Pakal ruled Palenque from 615 to 683 AD; he died around age 80. The tomb was discovered in 1952 by archaeologist Alberto Ruz Lhuillier. The lid carving shows Pakal at the moment of death, surrounded by Mayan cosmology — the Tree of Life, the celestial bird, and the maw of the underworld.

question: Deep in the rainforest of northern Guatemala rises the great Classic Mayan city of Tikal — five steep limestone temple-pyramids piercing the jungle canopy, with about 3,000 buildings in total. The city flourished from about 200 to 900 AD. About how tall is the tallest pyramid (Temple IV)?
context: Temple IV is the tallest pre-Columbian structure in the Americas. From its top, the canopy stretches to the horizon — used for the rebel base scene in Star Wars (1977). Tikal collapsed around 900 AD along with the rest of the southern Maya lowlands, for reasons including drought and over-population.

question: In western Honduras, a Classic Mayan city's central plaza is dominated by a 21-metre staircase whose risers carry the longest single Mayan hieroglyphic inscription anywhere — about 2,200 glyphs telling the dynastic history of the city. The staircase was reassembled in the 1930s after centuries of jungle collapse. What city is this?
context: The inscription is fragmentary — the order of many blocks was lost when the staircase collapsed. Reading order is debated, but the broad outlines of Copan's 17 known kings have been recovered. Copan was famous for its sculptural style, including portrait stelae of each king.

question: At the Postclassic Mayan city of Chichen Itza in Mexico's Yucatan, a stepped pyramid dedicated to the feathered serpent god displays a strange phenomenon at the spring and autumn equinoxes: descending shadows from the corners of the pyramid create a serpent slithering down the staircase to a stone serpent head at the base. What is the pyramid called?
context: Chichen Itza was inscribed as one of the 'new seven wonders of the world' in a 2007 popular vote. The pyramid was built around 800-900 AD over an older pyramid; modern excavation has confirmed the inner structure. Each of the four staircases has 91 steps; with the top platform, total is 365 — one per day of the year.

question: About 80 km south of Mérida in the Yucatán stands a Late Classic Mayan city built in a distinctive style of low-relief mosaic facades (the Puuc style). Its most spectacular building is the Governor's Palace — a 100-metre-long structure on a platform, with elaborate carved stone mosaic facade. What is this city called?
context: Uxmal's name in Yucatec Maya means 'built three times'. The site lacked the natural cenotes that supplied water elsewhere in the Yucatán; its inhabitants built chultunes (cisterns) under each plaza. UNESCO World Heritage 1996. The Adivino (Pyramid of the Magician) is a unique rounded pyramid built over five earlier phases.

question: On a flattened hilltop above the Oaxaca Valley sits a vast 500 BC-750 AD Zapotec city — terraced platforms, pyramids, and an unusual arrow-shaped building thought to be an astronomical observatory. The hilltop has no natural water source; the inhabitants captured rainfall. What is this city called?
context: Monte Alban was the capital of the Zapotec culture, dominating southern Mexico while Teotihuacan dominated the central highlands. The 'Danzantes' carvings — over 300 stone slabs depicting twisted human figures — were originally interpreted as dancers but are now generally understood as defeated rivals.

question: About 45 km southeast of Oaxaca city in Mexico, a Zapotec-Mixtec site has buildings whose external walls are decorated with thousands of finely fitted small stone pieces forming intricate geometric mosaics — no two are alike. Spanish friars demolished the main religious complex to build a colonial church on top. What is this site called?
context: Mitla means 'place of the dead' in Nahuatl; the Zapotec name was Lyobaa, 'place of rest'. The geometric facades use the step-fret and Greek-key patterns repeatedly. The Mixteca-Puebla style was influenced by Zapotec and Mixtec contact in the Postclassic period.

question: Across the Mississippi from St Louis in Illinois sit the earthworks of the largest pre-Columbian city in North America, peaking around 1100 AD with about 20,000 inhabitants. Its central earthen Monks Mound is the largest pyramid by base area in the Americas — 290 metres long, 30 metres tall. What is this city called?
context: Cahokia covered about 16 sq km. The city built more than 120 mounds, of which about 80 remain. It declined around 1300, possibly from over-resource extraction, flooding, or political fragmentation. The 'Woodhenge' wooden circles served as a solar calendar. UNESCO World Heritage 1982.

question: In the southwestern corner of Colorado, hundreds of stone-and-mortar 'apartment buildings' are tucked into natural alcoves under overhanging cliffs — built by the Ancestral Puebloan people between roughly 600 and 1300 AD. The largest, Cliff Palace, has 150 rooms in a 3-storey structure under one massive cliff overhang. What is this national park called?
context: The cliff dwellings were occupied for about a century around 1190-1290 before mass abandonment. Drought, deforestation, and conflict are all hypothesised. Modern Pueblo peoples (Hopi, Zuni, Acoma) consider Mesa Verde and other ancestral sites part of their lineage. UNESCO World Heritage 1978.

question: In a remote canyon in northwest New Mexico, a 9th-12th-century Pueblo culture built massive multi-storey stone 'great houses' linked by 600 km of straight built roads radiating outward into the desert. The site's astronomical alignments are remarkable — Pueblo Bonito tracks lunar standstills, solar solstices, and equinoxes. What is the site called?
context: Chaco's 'great houses' include over 800 rooms in Pueblo Bonito alone — five storeys, D-shaped plan, vast central plaza. The 'Sun Dagger' petroglyph on Fajada Butte uses solar light slits to mark equinoxes and solstices. UNESCO World Heritage 1987.

question: In northern New Mexico stands a multi-storey adobe Pueblo community that has been continuously inhabited for over 1,000 years — making it one of the oldest continuously inhabited communities in the United States. The connected adobe structures rise up to five storeys. What is the community called?
context: Acoma Pueblo also claims continuous occupation for at least 1,000 years; both compete for 'oldest'. Taos Pueblo's adobe buildings are still occupied by Taos Pueblo tribal members. The houses traditionally had no doors at ground level — entry was through ceiling hatches via ladders that could be pulled up for defence. UNESCO World Heritage 1992.

question: In a desert valley about 200 km north of Lima, Peru, lies the oldest known city in the Americas — six earthen pyramids, plazas, residential complexes, dating to about 3000-2000 BC. It is roughly contemporaneous with the great pyramids of Egypt and Mesopotamian Ur. What is this city called?
context: Caral was 'rediscovered' in 1994; excavation showed the absence of any pottery or military fortification — suggesting an unusually pacifistic, pre-ceramic urban culture. Quipu (knot-records) found at Caral predate Inca quipus by some 4,500 years. UNESCO World Heritage 2009.

question: In the highlands of north-central Peru, a 1500-200 BC ceremonial complex predates the Inca by 1,500 years. The El Lanzon stone — a 4-metre granite obelisk carved with a fanged anthropomorphic deity — stands in a hidden interior chamber. Acoustic engineering produced eerie roaring sounds through carved-stone channels. What is this site called?
context: Chavin priests apparently used psychoactive San Pedro cactus during the climactic rituals in the underground galleries. The acoustic engineering combined with hallucinogens, polished anthracite mirrors, and deliberate confusing architecture produced powerful religious experiences. UNESCO World Heritage 1985.

question: On a saddle between two peaks in the Peruvian Andes at 2,430 metres stands a perfectly preserved Inca royal estate, built around 1450 under emperor Pachacuti. Abandoned about a century later during the Spanish conquest, it was 'rediscovered' by Yale historian Hiram Bingham III in which year?
context: Bingham was actually searching for Vilcabamba — the last Inca stronghold against Spanish conquest. He was led to Machu Picchu by a local farmer; the site was not 'lost' to nearby Quechua people, only to outsiders. The Spanish probably never knew about it.

question: In the cloud-forest mountains of northern Peru sit the walled ruins of a 6th-16th-century fortress-city of the Chachapoyas culture — about 400 round stone-walled houses, surrounded by a 20-metre defensive wall (the highest pre-Columbian wall in the Americas). The Spanish chronicler Cieza de Leon called the Chachapoyas 'cloud warriors'. What is this site called?
context: The Chachapoyas were tall, light-skinned, mountain-dwelling people who resisted Inca conquest into the 1470s. Their mummies — found in cliff burials at Karajia, Laguna de los Condores, and elsewhere — show a population genetically distinct from surrounding peoples.

question: On the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia rose a major pre-Inca civilisation that flourished from about 500-1000 AD — its imperial reach extending across the Andean Altiplano. Its 'Gate of the Sun' and the underground 'Semi-subterranean Temple' show sophisticated stonework. What is this site called?
context: Tiwanaku declined around 1000-1100 AD, probably from prolonged drought. Its monumental stones (some up to 130 tons) are made of sandstone and andesite quarried 10-90 km away. The Gate of the Sun is carved from a single 10-ton andesite block.

question: On Easter Island (Rapa Nui), about 900 large stone statues called moai were carved between roughly 1100 and 1600 AD by the indigenous Polynesian inhabitants. Each was moved (sometimes many kilometres) from the volcanic-tuff quarry of Rano Raraku to its ahu platform on the coast. What's the leading current theory for how they were moved?
answer: 'Walked' upright by rocking them side-to-side with ropes
choices: 'Walked' upright by rocking them side-to-side with ropes
Carried on flat wooden sledges with rollers
Floated upstream on rafts in narrow inland channels
context: Experiments by archaeologists Carl Lipo and Terry Hunt show that 5-ton replicas can be 'walked' upright by teams of 18 people using three ropes — matching Rapa Nui legend that the moai 'walked' to their platforms. Earlier sledge-based theories required impossible numbers of trees.

question: Easter Island's indigenous Rapa Nui people developed (or independently invented) one of only three or four independent writing systems in human history — engraved on wooden tablets. About two dozen tablets survive in museums around the world; all of the rongorongo writers were killed or carried off by 19th-century Peruvian slavers. What language did the script encode?
answer: An archaic form of Rapa Nui (Polynesian)
choices: An archaic form of Rapa Nui (Polynesian)
An archaic form of Mayan glyphic
An archaic form of Sumerian cuneiform
context: Rongorongo remains undeciphered — the slave raids of 1862 destroyed the chain of knowledge before linguists could record it. The closest we have come is one tablet (the Mamari) which appears to contain a lunar calendar; the rest defies analysis.

question: In northern Ethiopia, the ancient capital of the Kingdom of Aksum (1st-7th centuries AD) contains a field of carved granite stelae marking royal graves. The standing stele of King Ezana is 24 metres tall; the longest collapsed stele was a single piece of stone 33 metres long — possibly the largest single-piece stone monument ever raised. When was the 24m King Ezana stele recovered to Aksum?
context: Mussolini took the 24m stele to Rome in 1937 as Italian war loot. Italy promised return in 1947 but delayed for decades. The pieces were finally flown back in 2005-08 and reerected in 2008. The 33m fallen stele has never been raised — moving it intact was impossible.

question: In central Mali stands the largest mud-brick building in the world — a vast 1907 reconstruction of an earlier 13th-century mosque. Wooden palm beams stick out of its walls as permanent scaffolding for the annual community-wide replastering ceremony. About how often is the entire mosque replastered?
context: The annual Crepissage de la Grande Mosquee is a festival — the whole town joins in. Men climb the protruding beams to spread fresh banco (mud + rice husk + shea butter) on the walls; women carry water; children carry mud. The mosque is part of the UNESCO old town of Djenne.

question: In the south Saharan trade town of Timbuktu in Mali, three universities (Sankore, Djinguereber, and Sidi Yahya, founded in the 14th-15th centuries) and dozens of private libraries hold up to 700,000 manuscripts on subjects from theology and law to astronomy, mathematics, medicine, and poetry. When jihadist militants seized Timbuktu in 2012, what happened to most of the manuscripts?
answer: Smuggled out to Bamako in oil drums and fertiliser sacks
choices: Smuggled out to Bamako in oil drums and fertiliser sacks
Confiscated and sold on the black market
Buried in the Sahara north of the city
context: Librarian Abdel Kader Haidara coordinated a rescue operation that moved over 350,000 manuscripts to safety in Bamako before the militants discovered them. After the French intervention pushed back the militants in 2013, manuscripts began returning. Many are now being digitised.

question: On the borders of South Africa, Botswana, and Zimbabwe, a 9th-13th-century kingdom predated Great Zimbabwe as the dominant African trading state of the region. Excavations of royal graves on Mapungubwe Hill recovered a famous golden rhino (sheet-gold over carved wood). What is the kingdom called?
context: The golden rhino (around 1250 AD) was found in 1932 with about a kilogram of gold leaf nails, beads, and other gold objects. The apartheid regime hid the find for decades; full disclosure came only after 1994. The Order of Mapungubwe is now South Africa's highest civilian honour.

question: Off the eastern coast of the Micronesian island of Pohnpei lies an artificial archipelago of about 100 islets built on a coral reef — its enormous basalt-and-coral wall structures rising up to 7 metres tall. The complex was the ceremonial centre of the Saudeleur dynasty from about 1100 to 1628. What is it called?
context: The basalt columns weigh up to 50 tons each and came from a quarry several kilometres away on the main island. How they were transported — over reefs and through tropical seas — remains unclear. Pohnpeian legend says twin sorcerers used magic to fly the stones into place. UNESCO World Heritage 2016, on in-Danger list 2016.

question: On the island of Tongatapu in Tonga stands a 12th-century trilithon (three-stone structure) — two upright coral-limestone monoliths supporting a horizontal stone, each weighing about 30-40 tons. The structure may have served as an astronomical observatory for solar alignments. What is it called?
context: Tongan legend says the demigod Maui carried the stones from across the sea. The structure aligns with the rising sun on the longest and shortest days of the year, suggesting solstice astronomy. Tongan king Taufa'ahau Tupou IV (in the 1970s) directed an investigation that confirmed the solar alignments.

question: On the Marquesas Islands (now in French Polynesia), large stone Tiki figures stand on stone platforms (paepae) throughout the islands. The Marquesas may have been the dispersal point for much of Polynesia — early voyaging from here likely settled Hawaii, Tahiti, and Easter Island. What human form does the Tiki represent?
context: Tiki figures show a stylised human form — large head, round eyes, hands on belly. They are sometimes considered representations of the first human or specific deified ancestors. Paul Gauguin lived and painted in the Marquesas in his last years; he is buried on Hiva Oa.

question: On the Hawaiian Islands, pre-contact Hawaiians built large stone-walled temple platforms (heiau) for religious ceremonies — agricultural, fertility, healing, and war. The largest are open enclosures of carefully fitted volcanic stones, sometimes hectares in area. Pu'ukohola Heiau on the Big Island was built around 1791 by Kamehameha I as part of his campaign to unify Hawaii. Why?
answer: An oracle had told him this temple would make him conqueror
choices: An oracle had told him this temple would make him conqueror
He wanted a defensive fortress against rival chiefs
It was a peace offering to the priesthood after a civil war
It marked the spot where he had landed his canoes
context: Kamehameha did indeed unite the Hawaiian islands by 1810. The temple was the largest heiau built in the Hawaiian Islands; it was completed in less than a year of forced labour. UNESCO World Heritage candidate; National Historic Site under the U.S. National Park Service.

question: On the Salisbury Plain in southern England stands a Neolithic-Bronze Age stone circle built in stages from about 3000 to 1500 BC. Two stone types: massive 25-ton local sandstone (sarsen) for the larger outer stones, and smaller 4-ton 'bluestones' that were transported from how far away?
answer: About 230 km from the Preseli Hills of Wales
choices: About 230 km from the Preseli Hills of Wales
About 50 km from the Mendip Hills of Somerset
About 100 km from the Cornish coast
About 5 km from the local Salisbury plain
context: The Preseli Hill origin of the bluestones was first proposed in 1923 and is now firmly established by geochemistry. How they were moved 230 km — possibly by raft along the coast then up rivers — remains contested. The site aligns with the summer solstice sunrise and the winter solstice sunset.

question: Even older than Lascaux, this French cave in the Ardèche, discovered in 1994, contains paintings dating to about 32,000-36,000 years ago — among the oldest known sophisticated cave art in the world. The animals depicted include rhinoceros, panthers, and mammoths — fauna not painted at Lascaux. What is this cave called?
context: Chauvet's art is sophisticated — shading, perspective, multiple horses in motion. Werner Herzog's 2010 documentary Cave of Forgotten Dreams shows the original cave; only a small number of researchers and approved visitors per year are now permitted. UNESCO World Heritage 2014.

question: In northern Spain, a cave whose ceiling is painted with about 20 polychrome bison was discovered by an aristocrat's 8-year-old daughter, Maria de Sautuola, in 1879. The shapes use natural rock contours for 3D effect. The paintings were initially dismissed as forgeries because they were too sophisticated; later analysis dated them to 14,000-19,000 years ago. What is the cave called?
context: The cave was closed to visitors in 2002 to protect the paintings; a replica was opened nearby. Don Marcelino Sautuola, Maria's father, presented the find at the 1880 Lisbon prehistory congress and was accused of fraud; he died in 1888 still disbelieved. Vindication came in the early 20th century.

question: Discovered in 1972 in a Bulgarian Black Sea coast cemetery, a Chalcolithic burial yielded the oldest large concentration of processed gold artefacts in the world — about 6 kg of gold beads, bracelets, and ornaments, dating to about 4600-4200 BC. The most lavish grave (Burial 43) belonged to a 40-50-year-old man. About when do the artefacts predate similar Egyptian gold work?
context: The Varna culture had organised metallurgy, ranked society, and intercontinental trade long before similar developments elsewhere. The cemetery has about 300 graves; only a small subset hold extreme wealth (suggesting hierarchy already in place). The Black Sea coast may have been a particularly favourable environment for early stratification.

question: In the limestone hills west of Luxor in Egypt, generations of New Kingdom pharaohs were buried in elaborate rock-cut tombs. About how many royal tombs have been catalogued in the Valley of the Kings since archaeological work began in the early 1800s?
context: KV5 — the tomb of the sons of Ramesses II — has at least 120 chambers, the largest tomb ever found in the Valley. KV62 (Tutankhamun) is the only intact royal tomb yet found. Archaeologists believe more tombs remain undiscovered; geophysical surveys continue.

question: In the Iraqi desert about 100 km southwest of Mosul stood a 1st-3rd-century Parthian-era fortress city famous for repelling sieges by Roman emperors Trajan and Septimius Severus. The city's circular walls (with 4 gates, 360 towers) were never breached during the Roman period. ISIS captured and destroyed major monuments in 2015. What is this city called?
context: Hatra fell only after the Sassanian Persian conquest in 240 AD. UNESCO World Heritage 1985. The Great Iwan and the central temples were dynamited by ISIS militants in 2015; major restoration work began after the city's liberation in 2017.

question: What we call 'the Great Wall' of China is actually multiple walls built by different Chinese dynasties at different times. Which dynasty built most of the wall that tourists visit today (the well-preserved brick-and-stone sections near Beijing)?
context: The Qin first dynasty connected earlier walls into something coherent; that 'first' wall was made mostly of rammed earth. The Han extended it. The Ming rebuilt and fortified the wall during their war with the Manchus in the 16th-17th centuries; that is the wall we see today.

question: In 2017, the ScanPyramids project used cosmic-ray muon tomography to detect a previously unknown structure inside the Great Pyramid of Giza — a long horizontal cavity above the Grand Gallery, about 30 metres long. The discovery was reported in 2017 (and refined in 2023). What was the nature of this discovery?
answer: A previously unknown internal cavity (purpose still debated)
choices: A previously unknown internal cavity (purpose still debated)
A hidden chamber containing Khufu's actual sarcophagus
A confirmed boat pit for the pharaoh's afterlife journey
An enormous internal scaffolding from construction
context: The 2017 paper in Nature announced a 'big void'. Whether it is a stress-relief cavity (a common Egyptian construction technique above heavy ceilings) or a sealed chamber is still debated. Subsequent work in 2023 found another corridor near the entrance. No one has entered either yet.

question: Across the dry coastal plain of southern Peru stretch hundreds of geoglyphs — straight lines, geometric shapes, and animal figures (a hummingbird, a monkey, a spider) up to 200 metres across, made by clearing surface stones to reveal lighter soil. The Nazca culture made them between roughly 500 BC and 500 AD. What is now the leading theory for their purpose?
answer: Ritual pathways related to water and mountain gods
choices: Ritual pathways related to water and mountain gods
Astronomical alignments for an ancient observatory
Landing strips for visiting ancient astronauts
Decorative art with no practical function
context: Anthropologist Maria Reiche spent her life mapping the lines (1940s-1990s) and arguing for astronomical alignments — most have not held up. Modern scholars favour ritual processional paths leading to water sources or sacred mountain shrines. The figures may have been seen by gods looking down from above.

question: Around 1346 BC, the heretical pharaoh Akhenaten moved Egypt's capital from Thebes to a new city in the desert he built from scratch on virgin land, dedicated to his god Aten. After his death his successors moved back to Thebes and the new city was abandoned within a generation. Where is the modern site of his capital located?
context: Akhenaten's reign and his single-deity worship of the sun-disc Aten was a radical religious revolution. His successors (Tutankhamun, Ay, Horemheb) reversed it. The fact that the city was abandoned almost immediately makes it an unusually pure archaeological snapshot of one moment in Egyptian history.

question: The largest of Rome's ancient public bath complexes, completed in 216 AD by Emperor Caracalla, could accommodate about 1,600 bathers at a time. The complex covered about 11 hectares. Underneath were corridors, furnaces, and water-supply chambers staffed by slaves. About what fraction of Rome's water did the baths consume?
choices: Roughly all of the city's water
context: Rome's eleven aqueducts brought about 1 billion litres per day. The Caracalla baths and the larger Diocletian baths (305 AD, 3,000 bathers) consumed a major portion of that water. The marble floors were heated by hypocaust — hot air circulating under raised floors and inside hollow walls.

question: Along the Appian Way in 71 BC, the Roman general Marcus Licinius Crassus crucified about 6,000 followers of a defeated rebel leader — one every 35 metres for 200 km from Capua to Rome. Whom did he defeat?
answer: Spartacus and the Third Servile War rebels
choices: Spartacus and the Third Servile War rebels
context: The Third Servile War (73-71 BC) terrified Rome — slaves and gladiators rising in revolt. Spartacus himself died in battle; Crassus's grim demonstration along the Appian Way was meant to deter further uprisings. It worked: there were no more major slave revolts in Roman Italy.

question: The medieval Hindu Vijayanagara Empire in southern India was destroyed at one decisive battle in 1565. After this defeat, the victorious sultanate armies sacked and looted the capital city of Vijayanagara for six months. What was the battle called?
context: Five Deccan sultanates — Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, Golconda, Bidar, and Berar — temporarily united against the Vijayanagara king Ramaraya, who was beheaded on the battlefield. The empire never recovered; the ruins of Vijayanagara (now Hampi) are one of the most extensive archaeological sites in India. UNESCO World Heritage 1986.

question: Discovered in 1921 by Sir John Marshall and excavated alongside Mohenjo-daro, this Indus Valley city in modern Pakistani Punjab gave its name to the entire 2600-1900 BC Bronze Age civilisation that stretched across northern India and Pakistan. The civilisation's writing system, found stamped on small steatite seals, remains undeciphered. What is the site called?
context: The Indus civilisation covered about 1.25 million sq km — more than the contemporary Egyptian and Mesopotamian civilisations combined. Its cities had drainage systems and standardised brick sizes across hundreds of kilometres. Why it declined remains debated; theories include river shifts, climate change, and Aryan migration.

question: The 11th-13th-century medieval Sri Lankan capital flourished briefly under King Parakramabahu I, who rebuilt the irrigation system to support a vast rice economy and ordered the construction of the great Buddhist sculpture at Gal Vihara. The kingdom collapsed after his death. What is the capital called?
context: Polonnaruwa is east of the older Sri Lankan capital of Anuradhapura. The Parakrama Samudra ('Sea of Parakrama') reservoir built by the king covers about 14 sq km and still functions. The medieval Sinhalese had advanced irrigation engineering that supported one of the densest rural populations of the time.

question: In 1900-1901, sponge divers off the Greek island of Antikythera found a Roman shipwreck (around 65 BC) full of bronze and marble statues — and a mysterious corroded bronze mechanism with dozens of gears. Decades of X-ray and CT analysis have shown it was a complex astronomical computer modelling the motions of the Sun, Moon, and planets. What is it called?
context: The mechanism's gear-train sophistication was not matched by any other surviving artefact until 14th-century astronomical clocks. Whether it was a one-off masterpiece or one of many that did not survive remains debated. Its inscriptions describe eclipse predictions and the timing of the Greek Panhellenic games.

question: On the Libyan coast east of Tripoli sit the ruins of one of the most magnificent Roman provincial cities — birthplace of Emperor Septimius Severus (193-211 AD), who lavishly expanded it. Its forum, basilica, hunting baths, and theatre survive in good condition because the city was abandoned and partly buried in desert sand. What is it called?
context: Leptis Magna means 'Great Leptis' to distinguish it from another Phoenician town of the same name in Tunisia. UNESCO World Heritage 1982. The recent Libyan civil war (2011-) and ongoing instability have created concerns about looting and damage.

question: In the rough dockside neighbourhoods of late-19th-century Buenos Aires — La Boca, San Telmo, Barracas — Italian, Spanish, African Argentine, and rural gaucho immigrants combined polka, habanera, mazurka, and Andalusian musical traditions into a tightly embraced couple dance. The signature accordion-like instrument is what?
context: The bandoneon is a 19th-century German invention by Heinrich Band, originally intended for church music in poor parishes. German sailors brought them to Buenos Aires. Carlos Gardel — born in France, raised in Buenos Aires — became tango's first global star; his death in a 1935 plane crash was mourned across South America.

question: In the cotton-growing Mississippi Delta of the late 19th and early 20th centuries, African American sharecroppers, work-gang leaders, and prison labourers developed a musical form built on call-and-response field-hollers, blue notes (flattened 3rds and 7ths), and twelve-bar harmonic structures. What is this music called?
context: Robert Johnson, Charley Patton, Son House, and Skip James were the pillars of Delta blues. Most recorded music exists from the late 1920s-1930s; the music style is older. After WWII the Great Migration carried Delta blues to Chicago, where it electrified into Chicago blues — which then birthed rock and roll.

question: In the early-20th-century working-class neighbourhoods around the port of Rio de Janeiro, communities of formerly enslaved Afro-Brazilians and recent migrants from Bahia developed a percussion-driven dance music in 2/4 time, with cross-rhythmic patterns descended from West and Central African traditions. The annual Rio Carnaval parades feature competing schools. What is this music called?
context: Samba was nationalised as 'authentically Brazilian' under the Vargas government in the 1930s. The first samba schools (Mangueira, Portela) date from the late 1920s. The first samba recorded — 'Pelo Telefone' (1916) — credits Donga as composer; the song actually came out of the Pequena Africa neighbourhood community.

question: In late-1950s middle-class apartments along the beachfront in Rio's Ipanema and Copacabana neighbourhoods, a sophisticated jazz-influenced subgenre of samba emerged — quieter, more harmonically complex, sung in an intimate murmur. 'Chega de Saudade' (1958) by Joao Gilberto is often called its first record. Who was the great composer who wrote 'The Girl from Ipanema'?
answer: Antonio Carlos Jobim (with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes)
choices: Antonio Carlos Jobim (with lyricist Vinicius de Moraes)
context: Jobim and de Moraes wrote 'Garota de Ipanema' in 1962 about a teenager (Heloisa Pinheiro, then 17) who walked past their Veloso bar. The Stan Getz / Joao Gilberto / Astrud Gilberto 1964 recording became one of the best-selling jazz records of all time.

question: In the late 1960s in the South Bronx, Spanish Harlem, and the Lower East Side of New York, Cuban and Puerto Rican immigrant musicians fused son montuno, mambo, and other Caribbean styles with bigger-band American jazz arrangements. The Fania Records label commercialised the new sound. What was the new style called?
context: Salsa was both new and a marketing name — much of it derived from Cuban son. The Cuban Revolution (1959) cut off the Cuban music industry, opening space for Puerto Rican and Cuban-American musicians (Hector Lavoe, Ruben Blades, Willie Colon) to define the genre. 'Salsa' was popularised by Izzy Sanabria and Fania promoters around 1973.

question: In the urban port neighbourhoods of late-19th-century Havana and Matanzas, Cuba, descendants of West African slaves developed a percussion-and-vocal music that fused Spanish décima poetic verse, Yoruba rhythmic ideas, and Cuban-Caribbean settings. The dance imitates a chicken courting a hen. What is this music called?
context: Three styles of Cuban rumba exist: yambu (slowest, no rooster step), guaguanco (with the rooster step), and columbia (a fast male solo). UNESCO inscribed Cuban rumba as Intangible Heritage in 2016. 'Ballroom rumba' as taught in Western dance schools is a different (much slower) style not related to traditional rumba except by name.

question: In the Dominican Republic in the mid-19th century, a couple dance in 2/4 time with rapid hip motion and a distinctive 'walking' step came out of countryside music played by accordion-guira-tambora trios. Generalissimo Trujillo promoted it as the national music in the 1930s. What is it called?
context: The dance step's slight limp is sometimes said to honour a wounded general (or a one-legged sugar-cane worker), but is just a stylised hip motion. Merengue's three traditional instruments — accordion, guira (metal scraper), and tambora drum — define the perico ripiao folk style. Modern merengue uses electric instruments.

question: Born in the rural Dominican Republic in the early 20th century, this guitar-based music was long considered low-class music of bars and brothels — banned from radio play until the 1980s. Bachateros sing of unrequited love (amargo). What is the music called?
context: Trujillo and his successors banned bachata from radio. Juan Luis Guerra and his 1990 album 'Bachata Rosa' transformed it into respectable music. Today bachata is a global Latin pop genre; the original 'amargue' (bitter) style is still played in country bars.

question: In southern Spain's Andalusian region, three centuries of overlap among Gitano (Romani), Moorish, Jewish, and Christian Iberian cultures gave rise to a passionate music-and-dance form combining cante (singing), toque (guitar), and baile (dance). The music's twelve-beat cycle alternates between binary and ternary feel. What is this art form called?
context: Flamenco palos (styles) include solea (deep, sorrowful), buleria (fast, festive), seguiriya (tragic), tangos (rhythmic, danceable), and many others. UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2010. The original flamenco was sung without instrumental accompaniment ('cante a palo seco') — the guitar entered later.

question: In the working-class districts of Lisbon (Alfama, Mouraria, Bairro Alto) in the early 19th century, a melancholic urban folk music developed — sung by a solo singer (fadista) accompanied by a 12-string Portuguese guitar (guitarra portuguesa) and a 6-string viola. Its central emotional theme is 'saudade' — yearning, longing, and loss. What is this music called?
context: Fado has two main styles — Lisbon fado (sad, melancholic) and Coimbra fado (academic, performed by male students). Amalia Rodrigues (1920-1999) was the genre's defining 20th-century voice. UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2011. The 12-string Portuguese guitar developed in the 19th century from older cittern designs.

question: In the Appalachian region of the American South in the 1920s-1930s, a popular music genre emerged from English, Scottish, and Irish ballad traditions combined with African American fiddle and banjo styles. The 1927 Bristol Sessions in Tennessee — where Jimmie Rodgers and the Carter Family were first recorded — are often called the genre's 'big bang'. What was it called?
context: The Carter Family standardised country as a recordable commercial form. Nashville became the industry's centre after WWII, when the Grand Ole Opry radio show drew record labels. Country diverges from bluegrass mainly in the use of pedal steel and electric guitar.

question: In the South Bronx of New York City on 11 August 1973, Jamaican-American teenager Clive 'Kool Herc' Campbell DJed his sister's back-to-school party at 1520 Sedgwick Avenue, extending the 'break' (instrumental drum sections) of funk records by switching between two turntables. The party is generally credited as the birth of which musical genre?
context: The four pillars of hip-hop culture were named by Afrika Bambaataa around 1974: DJing, MCing (rapping), b-boying (breakdancing), and graffiti. The Sugarhill Gang's 'Rapper's Delight' (1979) was the first hip-hop record to chart. 1520 Sedgwick Avenue is recognised on the New York register of historic places.

question: In late-1950s Jamaica, just before reggae emerged, local musicians took American R&B and combined it with mento (Jamaican folk) and Caribbean calypso, producing an upbeat-on-the-offbeat style with a strong horn section. What is this earlier genre called?
context: Ska in turn evolved into rocksteady (slower, around 1966-1968) and then reggae (slower still, late 1960s). British 2-tone ska revival in 1979-1981 (The Specials, Madness, The Beat) and American third-wave ska in the 1990s (No Doubt, Sublime) gave the genre two further global lives.

question: In late-19th and early-20th-century Trinidad, a topical song form developed in the African-Caribbean community for the annual Carnival, using satire and double-entendre to comment on contemporary politics and gossip. Trinidad's first calypsonian to record was the Roaring Lion. What is the song form called?
context: Calypsonians compete in calypso tents during the lead-up to Carnival. Mighty Sparrow, Lord Kitchener, and Black Stalin are among the great calypsonians of the 20th century. Soca developed from calypso in the 1970s by adding African and Indian rhythms — it now dominates Trinidad Carnival.

question: In 1830s Bohemia, a fast 2/4 couple dance with a hop on the offbeat became the most popular European social dance of the mid-19th century — spreading from Prague to Paris, London, and on to immigrant communities in the Americas. What dance is this?
context: The polka swept through Europe so fast that by 1844 the press wrote of 'polkamania'. The dance is named possibly from 'pulka' (Czech for 'half', referring to the half-step), or from 'Polka' (a Polish woman — the dance is Czech, not Polish, despite the name). Czech and Polish polkas remain alive in Texas and Wisconsin via immigrant communities.

question: Originating in temples of Tamil Nadu in southern India over 2,000 years ago, a classical dance form combines rhythmic footwork (nritta), expressive storytelling (nritya), and dramatic mime (natya). The dance was originally performed by female temple servants (devadasis) and was banned by the British in the early 20th century before being revived. What is its name?
context: Rukmini Devi Arundale and others led the revival of bharatanatyam in the 1930s, removing devadasi-system associations and making it a respectable middle-class accomplishment. The repertoire follows a standard order — alarippu, jatiswaram, shabdam, varnam, padam, tillana.

question: On the Indonesian islands of Java and Bali, traditional ensembles of bronze percussion (gongs, metallophones, drums), bamboo flutes, and stringed instruments play complex layered music for court, religious, and dance ceremonies. Composers Debussy and Satie heard one at the 1889 Paris World Exposition and influenced French Impressionism. What is this orchestra called?
context: Javanese gamelan tends to be slower and meditative; Balinese gamelan is faster and more dramatic. The tuning systems (slendro, pelog) are pentatonic and heptatonic respectively — neither matches Western tempered tuning. UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2021.

question: In early-17th-century Japan, a new theatrical form combining stylised dance, song, mime, and elaborate makeup developed for the urban merchant class. After scandals involving women and boy performers, the shogun restricted performance to adult male actors only. What is this theatre called?
context: Kabuki actors are all male; female roles are played by 'onnagata' specialists. The art is highly stylised — distinctive makeup (kumadori), elongated gestures, and exaggerated vocal delivery (mie). UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2008. The signature revolving stage was invented for kabuki in the 18th century.

question: Japan's oldest continuous theatrical art form, developed in the 14th century from earlier folk and religious performance, combines slow, stylised mime, masked actors, sung text, and a four-instrument orchestra (one flute, three drums). What is the theatre called?
context: Noh masks are works of art — the angle at which they tilt changes their apparent expression. Plays are categorised by main character: god (kami), warrior (shura), woman (kazura), miscellaneous, or demon (kiri). UNESCO recognised Nohgaku (Noh and Kyogen) as Intangible Heritage 2001.

question: In the Russian republic of Tuva, just north of Mongolia, traditional male singers produce two or three pitches simultaneously — a deep fundamental and one or two whistling overtones — by precisely shaping the vocal tract. What is this called?
context: Different styles (sygyt, kargyraa, khoomei proper) emphasise different overtone bands. The Tuvan ensemble Huun-Huur-Tu has toured globally. Frank Zappa and Paul Pena (who taught himself by listening to shortwave radio) helped introduce throat singing to Western audiences.

question: In the Indian subcontinent, a devotional Muslim Sufi music tradition — about 700 years old — features lead singers, harmonium, dholak drums, and clapping audience participation. Songs praise God, the Prophet, and Sufi saints. Pakistani performer Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan was its global ambassador. What is this music called?
context: Amir Khusrau (1253-1325) is sometimes credited with founding qawwali at the Sufi shrine of Nizamuddin Auliya in Delhi. The music is performed at Sufi shrines (dargahs) on the urs anniversaries of saints. Khan's collaboration with Peter Gabriel introduced qawwali to Western pop audiences.

question: In late-1960s Nigeria, multi-instrumentalist Fela Anikulapo-Kuti developed a politically charged dance music that fused Yoruba percussion, jazz horns, funk grooves, and lengthy improvisation. His compound 'Kalakuta Republic' became both nightclub and political headquarters. What is this music called?
context: Fela was repeatedly arrested by the Nigerian military government. His mother, the activist Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti, was killed when soldiers raided Kalakuta in 1977. Afrobeat is distinguished from 'Afrobeats' (with the 's', a 21st-century Nigerian pop genre) — Fela's son Femi Kuti and grandson Made Kuti are major contemporary Afrobeat artists.

question: In Zimbabwe and southern Africa, the Shona people play a hand-held thumb piano made of metal tongues fixed to a wooden soundboard, often inside a calabash resonator. The instrument is used in spirit-possession ceremonies. What is it called?
context: The mbira dzavadzimu (mbira of the ancestors) is used in bira ceremonies where mediums call ancestral spirits. The mbira survives despite a missionary campaign that classified it as 'devil's music' through much of the 20th century. Master player Stella Chiweshe and groups like Mhuri yekwaRwizi have brought mbira to global audiences.

question: In Morocco, descendants of West African slaves brought through trans-Saharan slave routes maintain a Sufi-influenced trance ritual music using long iron castanets (qraqab), three-stringed bass lute (guembri), and call-and-response singing. The annual Gnaoua and World Music Festival is held in Essaouira. What is the tradition called?
context: Gnawa music accompanies the lila — an all-night spiritual ceremony to heal possession or call beneficial spirits. Each song is dedicated to a specific spiritual figure (mluk). UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2019.

question: The tomato, fundamental to Italian cuisine since the 18th century, is actually a New World plant — domesticated in pre-Columbian times in which region?
answer: The Andean region of South America
choices: The Andean region of South America
The Mississippi Valley of North America
The Mediterranean coast of southern Italy
context: Wild tomatoes still grow in Peru, Ecuador, and northern Chile.
